name: Thales of Miletus
bio: Traditionally the first Greek philosopher, Thales proposed that water is the originating principle of all things and so explained the world by nature rather than by the gods.
bio_full: Thales lived in Miletus, a rich trading city on the Ionian coast of what is now Turkey, in the early sixth century BC. He wrote nothing that survives, and everything we know comes from later reports, chiefly Aristotle and Herodotus. Ancient tradition counted him among the Seven Sages and credited him with practical feats: predicting a solar eclipse (usually linked to 585 BC), measuring the height of the pyramids by their shadows, and cornering the market in olive presses to show that philosophers could grow rich if they wanted to. None of his dates is secure.

Aristotle names Thales as the founder of natural philosophy because he said the archē, the origin and underlying stuff of everything, is water, and that the earth floats on water. The claim matters less for its content than for its form: a single natural principle offered to explain the many things we see, open to argument and correction. He is also reported to have said that all things are full of gods and that the magnet has a soul because it moves iron. His pupils and successors in Miletus, Anaximander and Anaximenes, criticised and replaced his answer, beginning the tradition of rational debate that runs through Greek philosophy.

name: Pythagoras
bio: A religious teacher and founder of a brotherhood in southern Italy, Pythagoras taught the immortality and transmigration of the soul; later followers made number and harmony the key to the cosmos.
bio_full: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos and emigrated around 530 BC to Croton in southern Italy, where he founded a community that was part philosophical school and part religious order, with rules of diet, silence and secrecy. The community gained political power in several Greek cities of Italy and later provoked violent reaction. He wrote nothing, and ancient biographies written centuries later are full of legend, so his own teaching is hard to separate from that of his followers.

In his lifetime Pythagoras was famous chiefly as an expert on the fate of the soul, which he held to be immortal and reborn in other bodies, including animals. The idea that reality is structured by number, suggested by the simple ratios of musical harmony, was developed by later Pythagoreans such as Philolaus, and there is no secure evidence that Pythagoras himself proved the theorem that bears his name. Through Plato, who was deeply influenced by Pythagorean ideas, the vision of a mathematically ordered cosmos and an immortal soul passed into the mainstream of Western thought.

portrait_caption: Roman bust of Pythagoras

name: Heraclitus of Ephesus
bio: Heraclitus taught that everything is in ordered change governed by a rational Logos, that opposites are bound together, and that fire is the emblem of a world that changes by measure.
bio_full: Heraclitus came from an aristocratic family of Ephesus and flourished around 500 BC. He belonged to no school and was scornful of other thinkers, including Homer, Pythagoras and Xenophanes. He wrote a single book, which survives only in about a hundred short, often riddling fragments quoted by later authors; his compressed style earned him the nickname 'the Obscure'.

His central claim is that the world is ordered by a Logos, a rational account or law that most people fail to grasp although it is common to all. Opposites such as day and night, war and peace, the way up and the way down are aspects of one process held in tension. Fire, which lives by consuming and changes while keeping its measure, is his image of the cosmos. The famous saying that you cannot step into the same river twice is a later paraphrase; his own point concerned new waters flowing over the bather while the river stays the same. Plato, the Stoics, Hegel and Nietzsche all drew on him.
portrait_caption: Heraclitus, an imagined likeness in a later artwork

name: Parmenides of Elea
bio: Parmenides argued by pure deduction that what is cannot come to be, change or be divided, so that change and plurality are illusions; every later Greek philosopher had to answer him.
bio_full: Parmenides lived in Elea, a Greek colony on the west coast of southern Italy, and is said to have given the city its laws. Plato's dialogue Parmenides portrays him visiting Athens in old age and meeting a young Socrates, which would place his birth around 515 BC, though the meeting may be fictional. He set out his philosophy in a hexameter poem, often called On Nature, of which about 160 lines survive.

In the poem a goddess reveals two paths: the Way of Truth, which concerns only what is, and the Way of Opinion, the confused beliefs of mortals. Since what is not cannot be thought or spoken of, what is cannot have come into being from nothing, cannot perish, and cannot be divided or move. Reality is therefore one, whole and unchanging, and the world of change revealed by the senses is not to be trusted. The argument shocked Greek thought into a new rigour: Zeno defended it, Empedocles and the atomists tried to save change while granting its premises, and Plato's distinction between unchanging Forms and changing appearances is a response to it.
portrait_caption: Portrait head of Parmenides found at Velia (ancient Elea), 1st century AD

name: Zeno of Elea
bio: A pupil of Parmenides, Zeno devised paradoxes such as Achilles and the tortoise to show that belief in motion and plurality leads to absurdity.
bio_full: Zeno of Elea was the pupil, and according to Plato the younger companion, of Parmenides; his dates are inferred from Plato's account of their visit to Athens. Ancient sources report that he died bravely resisting a tyrant, though the details vary. He wrote a book of arguments, now lost, and his paradoxes are known mainly through Aristotle's Physics and the commentator Simplicius.

Zeno's method was to accept his opponents' assumptions and show that they lead to contradiction. If space and time are divisible, a runner must cross half a distance before the whole, and half of that half, endlessly (the Dichotomy); swift Achilles can never overtake the tortoise; and a flying arrow, at rest at every instant, never moves. Aristotle called him the inventor of dialectic. The paradoxes were discussed throughout antiquity and the Middle Ages, and mathematicians and philosophers still debate whether the modern theory of limits and infinite series fully resolves them.

portrait_caption: Engraving of a bust of Zeno of Elea, from Paradigmata graphices variorum artificum (Rijksmuseum)

name: Empedocles
bio: Empedocles explained the world as four eternal roots, earth, air, fire and water, mixed and separated by the cosmic forces of Love and Strife.
bio_full: Empedocles was a citizen of Acragas, a wealthy Greek city in Sicily, where he was active in politics and reportedly refused the offer of kingship. He was also a poet, physician and self-proclaimed wonder-worker. He wrote two hexameter poems, On Nature and Purifications, which survive in fragments, supplemented by a papyrus discovered in Strasbourg in the 1990s. Legend says he died by leaping into the crater of Mount Etna to prove he was immortal, but other ancient accounts have him dying in exile in the Peloponnese.

Accepting Parmenides' point that nothing comes from nothing, Empedocles held that the four roots never come into being or perish; what we call birth and death are only their mixing and separation. Love draws unlike things together and Strife pulls them apart, and the cosmos cycles endlessly between the rule of each. He also offered an early account of the evolution of living things from randomly combined parts, and a Pythagorean teaching of the soul's wanderings through many bodies. His four elements dominated Western natural philosophy until the seventeenth century.
portrait_caption: Empedocles, an imagined likeness in a later engraving

name: Democritus
bio: With his teacher Leucippus, Democritus founded atomism: everything consists of indivisible particles moving in empty space.
bio_full: Democritus came from Abdera, a Greek city on the north Aegean coast of Thrace, and travelled widely. Ancient catalogues list some seventy works on physics, mathematics, ethics, music and much else, but only fragments survive, many of them ethical maxims. Ancient sources make him implausibly long-lived, and his cheerful outlook earned him the later nickname 'the Laughing Philosopher'.

Atomism answered Parmenides by granting that what is cannot come from nothing, but allowing that the void, or what is not, exists too. Reality is countless uncuttable atoms, differing only in shape, arrangement and position, moving through the void and combining to form worlds. Qualities such as colour, sweetness and warmth exist only 'by convention'; in reality there are only atoms and void. His ethics aimed at euthymia, a cheerful and untroubled state of mind. Epicurus revived his physics, Lucretius put it into Latin verse, and atomism returned to science in the seventeenth century, though ancient atoms were argued for, not observed.
portrait_caption: Ancient Greek portrait bust identified as Democritus (cast in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow)

name: Protagoras and the Sophists
bio: The Sophists were paid itinerant teachers of rhetoric and civic skill; their most famous member, Protagoras, declared that man is the measure of all things.
bio_full: The Sophists were professional teachers who travelled through the Greek world in the fifth century BC offering instruction, for a fee, in rhetoric, argument and the skills needed for success in democratic politics. The best known are Protagoras of Abdera (c. 490–c. 420 BC), who spent long periods in Athens and was a friend of Pericles, and Gorgias of Leontini (c. 483–c. 375 BC), who came to Athens as an ambassador in 427 BC and dazzled audiences with his oratory. Most of what we know about them comes from Plato, who was hostile.

Protagoras taught that man is the measure of all things, which Plato read as a relativism about truth, and professed agnosticism about the gods. Gorgias argued, perhaps as a parody of Parmenides, that nothing exists, and praised the almost magical power of speech. The Sophists raised the great question of whether law and morality are natural or merely conventional. Plato's portrait made 'sophist' a term of abuse, but modern scholars treat them as serious thinkers who helped launch the study of language, education and political theory.
portrait_caption: Jusepe de Ribera, Protagoras, 1637

name: Socrates
bio: Socrates wrote nothing, yet his method of relentless questioning about virtue and the good life, and his execution by Athens, made him the founding figure of Western philosophy.
bio_full: Socrates was born in Athens around 470 BC, the son of a sculptor or stonemason and a midwife. He served as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian War and otherwise spent his life in public places questioning anyone willing to talk about courage, piety, justice and wisdom. He took no fees and lived in poverty. In 399 BC the restored democracy tried him for impiety and corrupting the young; he was found guilty and executed by drinking hemlock, refusing a chance to escape. Our knowledge comes from Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, whose portraits differ, so that reconstructing the historical Socrates is a famous scholarly problem.

Socrates' method, the elenchus, tests a person's definition of a virtue by drawing out its consequences until it contradicts something else they believe. He claimed to know only that he knew nothing, which the Delphic oracle reportedly called the greatest wisdom. He held that virtue is a kind of knowledge, that no one does wrong willingly, and that it is better to suffer injustice than to do it. His insistence that the unexamined life is not worth living turned philosophy from nature to ethics, and almost every later Greek school claimed him as its ancestor.
portrait_caption: Roman marble bust of Socrates, 1st century AD, Louvre

name: Plato
bio: Socrates' greatest pupil and founder of the Academy, Plato wrote dialogues that introduced the theory of Forms, the philosopher-king and the immortal soul, and set the agenda for Western philosophy.
bio_full: Plato was born into an aristocratic Athenian family and became a devoted follower of Socrates, whose execution in 399 BC turned him against existing politics. He travelled, perhaps to Egypt and certainly to southern Italy and Sicily, where he tried and failed to guide the tyrants of Syracuse toward philosophical rule. Around 387 BC he founded the Academy in a grove outside Athens, where Aristotle studied for twenty years. He died in Athens around 347 BC. Unusually for an ancient author, all his known works survive: some thirty-five dialogues and a set of letters of disputed authenticity.

Plato wrote dialogues, not treatises, so his own views must be inferred, and in the late works Socrates fades from the lead. His theory of Forms holds that behind the changing world of the senses stand eternal, unchanging patterns, such as Justice and Beauty themselves, which are the true objects of knowledge. The Republic links this to a soul of reason, spirit and appetite, a city ruled by philosophers and the allegory of the Cave. He criticised his own theory in the Parmenides. Through Aristotle, the Neoplatonists, Augustine and the Renaissance, his influence has been so pervasive that Whitehead called European philosophy a series of footnotes to Plato.
portrait_caption: Roman copy of Silanion's portrait of Plato, c. 370 BC, Capitoline Museums

name: Aristotle
bio: Plato's student and Alexander the Great's tutor, Aristotle founded formal logic and wrote foundational works on nature, metaphysics, ethics, politics and poetry.
bio_full: Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a physician to the Macedonian court. At seventeen he joined Plato's Academy in Athens and stayed twenty years, until Plato's death in 347 BC. He then spent time in Asia Minor and Lesbos doing pioneering biological research, and from 343 BC tutored the young Alexander of Macedon. Returning to Athens in 335 BC he founded his own school, the Lyceum, whose members were called Peripatetics. After Alexander's death in 323 BC anti-Macedonian feeling drove him to Chalcis, where he died the next year. His surviving works are mostly lecture notes; his polished dialogues are lost.

Aristotle grounded knowledge in this world rather than in separate Forms: things are compounds of matter and form, and to explain anything we need its four causes, material, formal, efficient and final. He invented the syllogism, classified animals, and wrote on physics, the soul, metaphysics, rhetoric and poetry. His ethics makes happiness, eudaimonia, a lifetime of activity in accordance with virtue, with each virtue a mean between extremes fixed by practical wisdom; his Politics calls humans political animals. Through Arabic and Latin commentators he became simply 'the Philosopher' for medieval thinkers, and his ethics was revived in twentieth-century virtue ethics.
portrait_caption: Roman copy of a Greek bronze bust of Aristotle by Lysippos, Palazzo Altemps, Rome

name: Diogenes of Sinope and the Cynics
bio: The Cynics, whose archetype was Diogenes of Sinope, lived philosophy as a public performance: needing almost nothing, flouting convention and calling themselves citizens of the world.
bio_full: Cynicism was inspired by Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates, but its defining figure was Diogenes of Sinope (c. 412/404–c. 323 BC). Exiled from his home city on the Black Sea after a scandal over defacing the coinage, he settled in Athens and later Corinth, living in poverty and famously sleeping in a large storage jar. Anecdotes, mostly preserved by Diogenes Laertius centuries later, show him begging, mocking Plato and telling Alexander the Great to stand out of his sunlight. His followers included Crates and Hipparchia, and Cynic preachers were familiar figures into the Roman Empire.

The name comes from the Greek for 'dog-like', an insult the Cynics embraced. They held that happiness lies in virtue and self-sufficiency, living according to nature rather than custom, and they attacked wealth, status, marriage conventions and political loyalties through shocking public behaviour. Asked where he came from, Diogenes is said to have called himself a citizen of the cosmos, the first recorded use of the idea of cosmopolitanism. Cynicism strongly influenced the Stoics, whose founder Zeno studied with Crates. The modern word 'cynical' has lost almost all of its original sense.
portrait_caption: Diogenes in a Roman mosaic, Römisch-Germanisches Museum, Cologne

name: Pyrrho of Elis and the Skeptics
bio: Pyrrho of Elis and his later followers held that we should suspend judgment about everything not evident, and that tranquillity follows as a result.
bio_full: Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360–c. 270 BC) was a painter turned philosopher who travelled to India with Alexander the Great's army, where he is said to have met ascetic sages. He wrote nothing; his ideas were recorded by his pupil Timon of Phlius. Two centuries later Aenesidemus revived 'Pyrrhonism' as a school, and around the late second century AD the physician Sextus Empiricus codified it in the Outlines of Pyrrhonism. A separate sceptical tradition flourished in Plato's Academy under Arcesilaus and Carneades.

Pyrrhonists did not claim that nothing can be known; that would itself be a dogma. Instead they set opposing arguments against one another until, finding them equally strong, they suspended judgment (epochē), and found that tranquillity of mind (ataraxia) followed. They lived by appearances, custom and nature without committing themselves on how things really are. The rediscovery of Sextus in the sixteenth century fuelled a sceptical crisis in European thought, through Montaigne, Descartes, Bayle and Hume.

portrait_caption: Pyrrho, from Illustrium philosophorum et sapientum effigies, 16th century

name: Epicurus
bio: Epicurus taught that the goal of life is pleasure understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental fear, grounded in an atomist physics with no divine interference and nothing to fear in death.
bio_full: Epicurus was born on Samos to Athenian parents and taught in Mytilene and Lampsacus before moving to Athens around 306 BC. There he bought a house and garden that gave his school its name, the Garden, and admitted women and slaves as members, which scandalised his contemporaries. He wrote prolifically, but apart from three letters and collections of maxims preserved by Diogenes Laertius, and charred papyri from Herculaneum, his works are lost. The Roman poet Lucretius gave the fullest surviving account of his system in On the Nature of Things.

Epicurus adopted Democritus' atoms and void, adding a slight random swerve to make room for freedom. The gods exist but take no interest in us; the soul is made of atoms and disperses at death, so that death is nothing to us. Pleasure is the beginning and end of the happy life, but the greatest pleasure is the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the mind, best achieved by simple living, friendship and withdrawal from politics. His 'fourfold remedy' summed it up: do not fear god or death; the good is easy to get and the terrible easy to endure. Despite the later sense of 'epicure', his ethics was austere.
portrait_caption: Roman bust of Epicurus, British Museum

name: Zeno of Citium and the Stoics
bio: Founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens, Stoicism taught that virtue is the only good and that happiness is living in agreement with a rational, providentially ordered nature.
bio_full: Zeno of Citium (c. 334–c. 262 BC) came to Athens from Cyprus, studied with the Cynic Crates and others, and around 300 BC began teaching in the Stoa Poikilē, the Painted Porch, which gave the school its name. His successors Cleanthes and above all Chrysippus (c. 279–c. 206 BC) built Stoicism into a complete system of logic, physics and ethics, and Panaetius and Posidonius later adapted it for Roman audiences. Almost all the works of the early Stoics are lost and are reconstructed from quotations and reports.

The Stoics held that the cosmos is a single living body pervaded by a rational principle, logos, identified with God and fate. Virtue, the perfection of reason, is the only good; health, wealth and reputation are 'indifferents', some preferable to others but irrelevant to happiness. Passions such as fear and anger are mistaken judgments that the wise person avoids, which is not the same as suppressing all feeling. Their logic anticipated modern propositional logic, and their idea of a natural law binding all rational beings fed into Roman law, Christian ethics and modern theories of human rights.
portrait_caption: Bust of Zeno of Citium, Farnese collection, Naples National Archaeological Museum (photo: Paolo Monti, 1969)

name: Seneca
bio: Statesman, dramatist and Stoic moralist, Seneca wrote letters and essays on anger, time, grief and providence that remain the most widely read Stoic prose.
bio_full: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born in Córdoba in Roman Spain and educated in Rome in rhetoric and philosophy. Exiled to Corsica by the emperor Claudius in AD 41, he was recalled in 49 to tutor the young Nero and became one of the most powerful and richest men in Rome during the first years of Nero's reign. He withdrew from court in 62 and was forced to commit suicide in 65 after being accused of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy. Critics ancient and modern have charged that his wealth and politics sat awkwardly with his philosophy.

Seneca's philosophical works include dialogues and essays such as On Anger, On the Shortness of Life and On Providence, and the 124 Moral Letters to Lucilius, written in his last years. He presents Stoicism as daily practice: self-examination each evening, rehearsal of misfortune, and the use of time as our only true possession. He also wrote tragedies that strongly influenced Renaissance drama. His letters were admired by early Christians, by Montaigne and by modern readers who come to Stoicism as a guide to living.

portrait_caption: Roman double herm of Socrates and Seneca, 3rd century AD, Antikensammlung Berlin

name: Epictetus
bio: A former slave who became the most influential Stoic teacher of his age, Epictetus taught that we should distinguish what is in our power, our own judgments and choices, from what is not.
bio_full: Epictetus was born a slave in Hierapolis in Phrygia and belonged to Epaphroditus, a freedman of Nero, in Rome. He was allowed to study with the Stoic Musonius Rufus and was later freed. When the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from Rome around AD 93, he moved to Nicopolis in western Greece and opened a school that attracted students from across the empire. He wrote nothing; his pupil Arrian recorded his lectures as the Discourses and condensed them into the Handbook (Enchiridion).

Epictetus' teaching turns on the dichotomy of control: our opinions, desires and choices are up to us, while body, property, reputation and office are not. Disturbance comes not from things but from our judgments about them, so freedom lies in training our assent and accepting what happens as part of a rational order. His blunt, vivid lectures made Stoicism a discipline open to slaves and emperors alike. Marcus Aurelius read him closely, the Handbook was adapted for Christian monks, and modern cognitive behavioural therapy acknowledges him as a forerunner.
portrait_file: Epicteti Enchiridion Latinis versibus adumbratum (Oxford 1715) frontispiece (cropped).jpg
portrait_caption: Imagined portrait of Epictetus, frontispiece to an edition of the Enchiridion, Oxford, 1715

name: Marcus Aurelius
bio: Roman emperor from 161 to 180, Marcus Aurelius wrote private notes to himself in Greek, the Meditations, which became the classic of practical Stoicism.
bio_full: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was born in Rome into a prominent family, adopted into the imperial house at the wish of Hadrian, and became emperor in 161, at first jointly with Lucius Verus. His reign was dominated by plague and by long wars on the Danube frontier against the Marcomanni and other peoples, and he died on campaign in 180. Taught by the Stoic Junius Rusticus, who lent him the works of Epictetus, he regarded philosophy as his true vocation.

The Meditations, written in Greek during his last decade and probably never meant for publication, record his effort to live by Stoic principles: to accept whatever nature brings, to treat others as fellow citizens of the cosmos, and to remember that every life, including an emperor's, is brief. Their themes of impermanence, the view from above and duty performed without complaint have given them a wide readership since their first printing in 1558. Historians note the tension between this philosophy and the harsh realities of his reign, including the persecution of Christians and the succession of his son Commodus.
portrait_caption: Marble bust of Marcus Aurelius, Musée Saint-Raymond, Toulouse

name: Plotinus
bio: Plotinus, founder of Neoplatonism, taught that all reality flows from an ineffable One through Intellect and Soul, and that philosophy is the soul's return to its source.
bio_full: Plotinus was born in Egypt, probably at Lycopolis, and studied for eleven years in Alexandria with the philosopher Ammonius Saccas. Hoping to learn Persian and Indian wisdom, he joined the emperor Gordian III's eastern campaign in 242–3, which ended in disaster. In 244 he settled in Rome and taught a circle that included senators and physicians. He began writing only at about fifty, and his pupil Porphyry arranged the fifty-four treatises into six groups of nine, the Enneads, and wrote his biography.

Plotinus saw himself as an interpreter of Plato. At the summit of reality is the One, or the Good, beyond being and thought. From it comes Intellect, which contains the Forms, and from Intellect comes Soul, which animates the cosmos; matter is the furthest point of this outflow, a privation rather than an evil creation. The human soul can turn inward and ascend through virtue and contemplation to union with the One, an experience Porphyry says Plotinus achieved four times. His thought shaped Augustine, Pseudo-Dionysius, Islamic philosophy and the Florentine Renaissance Platonists.
portrait_caption: Roman head traditionally identified as Plotinus, Museo Ostiense, Ostia

name: Augustine of Hippo
bio: Bishop of Hippo and the most influential Latin Church Father, Augustine fused Christianity with Platonism and wrote the Confessions and The City of God.
bio_full: Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste in Roman North Africa to a pagan father and a Christian mother, Monica. He studied rhetoric in Carthage, spent nine years as an adherent of the Manichaean religion, and taught rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan. In Milan, influenced by the sermons of Bishop Ambrose and by Neoplatonist books, he underwent the conversion described in the Confessions and was baptised in 387. Returning to Africa, he was ordained priest at Hippo Regius and became its bishop in 395 or 396, writing and preaching prolifically until his death in 430 while the Vandals besieged the city.

Augustine's thought is a Christian Platonism. Evil is not a substance but a privation of good; the will can be divided against itself; human beings cannot achieve goodness without divine grace, and through Adam's sin all inherit original sin. In the Confessions he explored memory and asked what time is, concluding that it is a distension of the mind. The City of God, written after the sack of Rome in 410, contrasts the earthly city built on love of self with the heavenly city built on love of God. He dominated Western theology for a thousand years and shaped Luther, Calvin, Descartes, Pascal and modern discussions of time and the self.
portrait_file: Saint Augustine by Philippe de Champaigne.jpg
portrait_caption: Philippe de Champaigne, Saint Augustine, c. 1645–50

name: Boethius
bio: A Roman senator executed by the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, Boethius translated Aristotle's logic into Latin and wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison.
bio_full: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was born into an old Roman senatorial family around 477–480, after the fall of the Western Empire, and became consul in 510 under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. He planned to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin and to show that they agreed, but completed only parts of Aristotle's logic with commentaries, along with textbooks on arithmetic and music and short theological treatises. In 522 he became Master of Offices, but he was soon accused of treason and magic, imprisoned near Pavia, and executed in 524 or 525.

In prison Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue in alternating prose and verse in which Lady Philosophy cures his despair by leading him to see that true happiness lies in God, that Fortune's wheel cannot touch the virtuous, and that divine foreknowledge, seen from eternity, does not destroy human freedom. His commentary on Porphyry's Isagoge posed the problem of universals for medieval philosophy, and his translations were the main source of Aristotelian logic in the Latin West until the twelfth century. The Consolation was among the most widely read books of the Middle Ages and was translated by Alfred the Great, Chaucer and Elizabeth I.
portrait_caption: Boethius, in a later depiction

name: John Scotus Eriugena
bio: The outstanding thinker of the Carolingian Renaissance, Eriugena translated Greek Christian Neoplatonists and wrote the Periphyseon, a vast system dividing all of nature, God included, into four kinds.
bio_full: John Scottus Eriugena, whose name means roughly 'the Irishman of Ireland', was born around 800 and had arrived in Francia by the 840s, where he taught at the court of Charles the Bald. Unusually for the time, he knew Greek, and he translated the works of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, Maximus the Confessor and Gregory of Nyssa into Latin. His treatise on predestination (851) was condemned at two church councils. Nothing reliable is known of his death, traditionally placed around 877.

His masterpiece, the Periphyseon or On the Division of Nature, divides nature into what creates and is not created (God as source), what is created and creates (the primordial causes), what is created and does not create (the world), and what neither creates nor is created (God as the end to which all returns). Drawing on Greek negative theology, he held that God is beyond all categories and so is better called 'nothing' than anything we can name. The work was condemned in 1225 for pantheism but influenced mystical and speculative thinkers including Nicholas of Cusa and, much later, the German idealists.

name: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
bio: Avicenna (Ibn Sina), physician and philosopher, built the most influential system of Islamic philosophy, with its distinction between essence and existence and its proof of a Necessary Existent.
bio_full: Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina was born in 980 near Bukhara, then capital of the Samanid state. A prodigy, he had mastered logic, mathematics and medicine by his late teens and was treating the Samanid ruler; he later said he understood Aristotle's Metaphysics only after reading a commentary by al-Farabi. Political turmoil drove him from court to court across Persia, where he served as physician and sometimes vizier, writing at night. He died in Hamadan in 1037. He wrote mainly in Arabic, with some works in Persian.

His encyclopaedic Book of Healing (al-Shifa) recast Aristotle with Neoplatonic elements. He distinguished a thing's essence, what it is, from its existence, that it is, and argued that the chain of contingent beings requires a Necessary Existent, identified with God. His 'Flying Man' thought experiment, a person created in mid-air with no sensations who would still be aware of himself, argued that the soul knows itself independently of the body. His Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries, and Latin translations of his philosophy deeply influenced Aquinas and Duns Scotus.
portrait_caption: Avicenna in a Persian miniature

name: Anselm of Canterbury
bio: Monk, abbot of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury, Anselm devised the ontological argument for God's existence and is often called the father of scholasticism.
bio_full: Anselm was born in Aosta in the Alps in 1033 and, after quarrelling with his father, crossed into France and joined the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy in 1060, attracted by the teacher Lanfranc. He became prior and then abbot of Bec, which he made a leading centre of learning. In 1093 he succeeded Lanfranc as Archbishop of Canterbury, and his struggles with the English kings William II and Henry I over the rights of the Church twice sent him into exile. He died in 1109 and was later canonised.

Anselm's motto was 'faith seeking understanding': he sought rational arguments for what he already believed. In the Proslogion (1077–78) he argued that God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived; since what exists in reality is greater than what exists only in the mind, such a being must exist. The monk Gaunilo objected at once with his perfect island, Aquinas rejected the argument, Descartes and Leibniz revived versions of it, and Kant's claim that existence is not a real predicate became the classic reply. In Why God Became Man he set out the satisfaction theory of the atonement.
portrait_caption: Anselm of Canterbury on his archiepiscopal seal (drawing)

name: Peter Abelard
bio: The most brilliant dialectician of the twelfth-century schools, Abelard offered a subtle solution to the problem of universals and an ethics based on intention, and is remembered too for his love affair with Héloïse.
bio_full: Peter Abelard was born in 1079 at Le Pallet in Brittany, the eldest son of a knight, and gave up his inheritance to study logic. He became the most celebrated teacher in Paris, defeating his own masters in public debate. His love affair with his pupil Héloïse, their secret marriage and the birth of their son ended when her uncle Fulbert had him castrated; both entered religious life. His theology was condemned at Soissons in 1121 and, after attacks led by Bernard of Clairvaux, at Sens in 1141. He died the next year on his way to appeal to Rome. His autobiography and the letters between him and Héloïse are classics of medieval literature.

On universals, Abelard argued that only individual things exist; universal words signify by reference to a common 'status' of things grasped by the mind, a position often called conceptualism or a sophisticated nominalism. His Sic et Non set contradictory authorities side by side to train students to resolve conflicts by analysis, a method that became central to scholasticism. In his Ethics, or Know Thyself, he argued that sin lies in the intention, the consent to what one knows is wrong, rather than in the act itself.
portrait_caption: Peter Abelard, imagined likeness in a later engraving

name: Hildegard of Bingen
bio: Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer and natural philosopher, Hildegard of Bingen wrote a trilogy of visionary theology and works on medicine and nature.
bio_full: Hildegard was born in 1098 into a noble family in the Rhineland and was given as a child to the religious life, being enclosed with the anchoress Jutta at the monastery of Disibodenberg. She became head of the women's community there in 1136 and around 1150 founded her own convent at Rupertsberg near Bingen, later adding a second at Eibingen. From 1141, with papal approval, she recorded the visions she had experienced since childhood. She corresponded with popes, emperors and Bernard of Clairvaux, made preaching tours, and died in 1179. She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

Her visionary trilogy, Scivias, the Book of Life's Merits and the Book of Divine Works, presents a cosmos in which God, nature and the human being mirror one another, illustrated with striking images. Central to her thought is viriditas, the 'greening' life force through which divine power renews creation. She also wrote on medicine and natural history, and composed a large body of liturgical songs and the morality play Ordo Virtutum. She is now read both as a major medieval woman writer and as an example of philosophy in a monastic rather than university setting.
portrait_caption: Hildegard of Bingen receiving a vision, from a medieval manuscript illumination

name: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
bio: Averroes (Ibn Rushd), judge and physician of Córdoba, wrote the great commentaries on Aristotle that made him simply 'the Commentator' to Latin scholars.
bio_full: Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Rushd was born in 1126 in Córdoba into a family of distinguished jurists. He trained in law, medicine and philosophy, and around 1169 was introduced to the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf, who asked him to explain Aristotle's works. He served as judge (qadi) in Seville and Córdoba and as court physician in Marrakesh. Late in life he fell from favour, was briefly exiled and his books were burned, but he was rehabilitated shortly before his death in Marrakesh in 1198.

Averroes wrote short, middle and long commentaries on almost all of Aristotle, seeking to recover the real Aristotle from Neoplatonic accretions. In the Decisive Treatise he argued that Islamic law commands philosophical study for those capable of it, and that demonstrative truth cannot conflict with scripture properly interpreted; in The Incoherence of the Incoherence he defended philosophy against al-Ghazali. His doctrine that there is one intellect for all humans caused fierce controversy when his works reached Paris, where 'Latin Averroism' was condemned in 1270 and 1277. His influence was much greater in Latin and Hebrew than in Arabic.
portrait_file: Andrea di bonaiuto, apoteosi di san tommaso d'aquino, 11 averroè.jpg
portrait_caption: Averroes, detail of Andrea di Bonaiuto's Triumph of St Thomas Aquinas, Santa Maria Novella, Florence, 1365–67

name: Maimonides
bio: Rabbi, physician and philosopher, Maimonides codified Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah and reconciled faith with Aristotelian philosophy in The Guide of the Perplexed.
bio_full: Moses ben Maimon was born in Córdoba, probably in 1138 (some traditions say 1135). When the Almohads conquered the city in 1148 and pressed Jews and Christians to convert, his family wandered through Spain and North Africa before settling in Fustat, near Cairo, around 1166. After his brother David drowned with the family fortune, Maimonides supported himself as a physician, eventually serving the court of Saladin's vizier, and became the leader of Egypt's Jewish community. He died in 1204 and was buried in Tiberias.

His Mishneh Torah (completed around 1178) organised the whole of Jewish law in clear Hebrew and remains authoritative. The Guide of the Perplexed (c. 1190), written in Judeo-Arabic for a student troubled by conflicts between scripture and philosophy, interprets biblical language about God figuratively and develops a negative theology: we can say what God is not, but not what God is. He argued that the eternity of the world could not be demonstrated either way and accepted creation on the basis of revelation. Aquinas cited him with respect as 'Rabbi Moses', and Spinoza both learned from and criticised him.
portrait_file: Portrait of Moses Maimonides in Thesaurus antiquitatum sacrarum.tif
portrait_caption: Imagined portrait of Maimonides, from Blasius Ugolinus, Thesaurus antiquitatum sacrarum, 18th century

name: Thomas Aquinas
bio: The Dominican friar Thomas Aquinas built the grandest synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy and Christian theology, including the Five Ways and a theory of natural law.
bio_full: Thomas was born around 1225 at Roccasecca, near Aquino, to a noble family who placed him as a boy at the abbey of Monte Cassino. Studying at Naples, he joined the new Dominican order in 1244 against his family's wishes; his brothers held him captive for about a year before relenting. He studied under Albert the Great at Paris and Cologne, became master of theology at Paris in 1256, and taught there and in Italy. In December 1273 he stopped writing after an experience during Mass, saying that all he had written seemed like straw. He died in 1274 on his way to the Council of Lyon and was canonised in 1323.

Aquinas held that reason and revelation cannot truly conflict. Using Aristotle, newly available in full, he distinguished essence from existence, argued in the Five Ways from motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and order to God, and treated the soul as the form of the body. His ethics joins Aristotle's virtues to the theological virtues, and his account of natural law, the rational creature's share in God's eternal law, became central to Catholic moral teaching and Western legal thought. The Summa Theologiae is his most famous work. Some of his positions were condemned in Paris in 1277, but he became the Church's official theologian, and Thomism revived strongly after 1879.
portrait_caption: Carlo Crivelli, Saint Thomas Aquinas, detail of the Demidoff Altarpiece, 1476

name: John Duns Scotus
bio: The Franciscan 'Subtle Doctor', Duns Scotus argued for the univocity of being, the formal distinction and individual 'thisness', and for the primacy of the will.
bio_full: John Duns Scotus was born around 1266, probably at Duns in the Scottish borders, and was ordained a Franciscan priest in 1291. He studied and lectured at Oxford and Paris, where he became regent master in theology in 1305, after a brief exile in 1303 for siding with the pope against King Philip IV of France. He was sent to Cologne in 1307 and died there the following year, aged about forty-two. His works, mostly commentaries on Peter Lombard's Sentences, survive in several versions and were left partly unfinished.

Scotus argued against Aquinas that 'being' is said univocally, in the same sense, of God and creatures, so that natural reason can form a concept of God. He introduced the formal distinction, between aspects of a thing that are really one but conceptually distinct, and haecceity or 'thisness', the principle that makes an individual this individual rather than another. He stressed the freedom of the divine and human will and gave a powerful version of the argument for a first cause. His followers, the Scotists, were a major school; Renaissance humanists mocked them, giving English the word 'dunce'.
portrait_caption: Imagined portrait of John Duns Scotus, 15th century

name: William of Ockham
bio: The Franciscan logician William of Ockham championed nominalism and the principle of parsimony known as Ockham's Razor, and defended the separation of spiritual and secular power.
bio_full: William was born around 1287 in the village of Ockham in Surrey and joined the Franciscans young. He studied theology at Oxford but never became a regent master, hence his title 'Venerable Inceptor'. Summoned to the papal court at Avignon in 1324 to answer charges of heresy, he became involved in the dispute over Franciscan poverty and in 1328 fled with the head of his order to the protection of Emperor Louis of Bavaria. He was excommunicated, spent his last two decades in Munich writing against the papacy, and died there in 1347, possibly of the Black Death.

Ockham held that only individual things exist; universals are concepts, natural signs in the mind that signify many individuals. His Summa of Logic develops a theory of mental language and of how terms stand for things. The 'razor', a principle that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity (the famous wording is later, though the idea is his), let him strip away many scholastic entities. He held that God's existence and many theological truths cannot be demonstrated, only believed. His nominalism dominated the late medieval 'modern way' and influenced the empiricists, and his political writings anticipated theories of limited government.
portrait_caption: Sketch labelled 'frater Occham iste' from a manuscript of Ockham's Summa logicae, 1341

name: Nicholas of Cusa
bio: Cardinal and mathematician, Nicholas of Cusa taught 'learned ignorance': precise knowledge of God is impossible, and in God all opposites coincide.
bio_full: Nicholas Krebs was born in 1401 at Kues (Latin Cusa) on the Moselle, the son of a prosperous boatman. He studied at Heidelberg, Padua, where he took a doctorate in canon law, and Cologne. At the Council of Basel he first supported the council against the pope, then switched to the papal side and in 1437 joined a mission to Constantinople to negotiate church union. He became a cardinal in 1448 and bishop of Brixen in the Tyrol, where he clashed with the local duke. He died at Todi in 1464 while preparing a crusade.

On Learned Ignorance (1440) argues that the finite mind can never grasp the infinite exactly, as a polygon with ever more sides approaches but never becomes a circle; wisdom begins in knowing this ignorance. In God, the absolute maximum, all opposites coincide. He also argued that the universe has no fixed centre or boundary and that the earth is not at rest, ideas later echoed by Giordano Bruno. His work On the Peace of Faith imagined a dialogue among religions. He stands at the turn from medieval to Renaissance thought.
portrait_caption: Nicholas of Cusa, detail of an altarpiece in the hospital chapel at Kues

name: Niccolò Machiavelli
bio: Florentine diplomat and political writer, Machiavelli analysed power as it actually works in The Prince and defended free republics in the Discourses on Livy.
bio_full: Niccolò Machiavelli was born in Florence in 1469 and received a humanist education. After the fall of Savonarola in 1498 he became secretary of the Second Chancery of the Florentine republic, serving for fourteen years on diplomatic missions to Cesare Borgia, Louis XII of France, the emperor and the pope, and organising a citizen militia. When the Medici returned in 1512 he was dismissed, and in 1513 he was imprisoned and tortured on suspicion of conspiracy. In enforced retirement on his farm near San Casciano he wrote The Prince, the Discourses on Livy, The Art of War, the comedy Mandragola and, later, the Florentine Histories. He died in 1527.

Machiavelli set out to describe the 'effectual truth' of politics rather than imagined republics. In The Prince (written 1513, published 1532) a ruler needs virtù, the energy and skill to master fortuna, and must be willing to act against conventional morality when the preservation of the state requires it. The Discourses argue that republics with armed, participating citizens and institutionalised conflict between nobles and people are more durable than principalities. Condemned for centuries as a teacher of evil, which gave English the word 'Machiavellian', he is now read as a founder of modern political science and a major theorist of republican liberty, though how to reconcile the two books is still debated.
portrait_file: Portrait of Niccolò Machiavelli by Santi di Tito.jpg
portrait_caption: Santi di Tito, portrait of Niccolò Machiavelli, late 16th century, Palazzo Vecchio, Florence

name: Michel de Montaigne
bio: Montaigne invented the essay as a form of self-examination and revived ancient scepticism, summing up his outlook in the motto 'What do I know?'
bio_full: Michel Eyquem de Montaigne was born in 1533 at the family château near Bordeaux, into a recently ennobled merchant family. His father had him taught Latin as his first language. He studied law, served as a magistrate in the Bordeaux parlement, and formed an intense friendship with Étienne de La Boétie, whose death in 1563 devastated him. In 1571 he retired to his tower library to read and write. He travelled through Germany and Italy in 1580–81, served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux, and acted as a go-between during the French Wars of Religion. He died at his château in 1592.

The Essays, first published in 1580 and expanded until his death, are 'attempts' or trials of his judgment on every subject, from cannibals and cruelty to friendship, experience and death. Taking himself as his subject, body, moods, contradictions and all, he made the changing individual a theme of philosophy. His 'Apology for Raymond Sebond' popularised Pyrrhonian doubt, and his essays on custom and on the peoples of the New World question European assumptions of superiority. He shaped Shakespeare, Pascal, Descartes and the whole tradition of the personal essay.
portrait_file: Portrait of Michel de Montaigne, circa unknown.jpg
portrait_caption: Portrait of Michel de Montaigne, anonymous, late 16th century

name: Francis Bacon
bio: Lawyer, statesman and herald of the new experimental science, Francis Bacon diagnosed the 'idols' that distort the mind and proposed a reformed method of induction.
bio_full: Francis Bacon was born in London in 1561, the son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal. He studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, trained as a lawyer, and entered Parliament in 1581. His rise was slow under Elizabeth I but rapid under James I: he became Solicitor General, Attorney General, Lord Keeper and, in 1618, Lord Chancellor, as Viscount St Alban. In 1621 he was convicted of accepting bribes and removed from office. He spent his last years writing and died in 1626, by tradition of a chill caught while stuffing a chicken with snow to test refrigeration.

Bacon planned a 'Great Instauration', a complete renewal of knowledge, of which the Novum Organum (1620) was the methodological part. It warns against four 'idols' of the mind, of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre, and proposes an induction that climbs gradually from carefully collected observations, using negative instances, rather than leaping to general axioms. He held that knowledge should serve human welfare, an idea captured in the phrase 'knowledge is power'. His utopia New Atlantis imagined a state-funded research institution that inspired the founders of the Royal Society. He also wrote the Essays and The Advancement of Learning.
portrait_caption: Paul van Somer I, portrait of Francis Bacon, 1617

name: Thomas Hobbes
bio: Hobbes built a materialist philosophy and, in Leviathan, argued that only an absolute sovereign can rescue humans from a war of all against all.
bio_full: Thomas Hobbes was born in 1588 in Malmesbury, Wiltshire, prematurely, he later said, because his mother was frightened by news of the Spanish Armada, so that 'fear and I were born twins'. After Oxford he became tutor and secretary to the Cavendish family, earls of Devonshire, a connection that lasted all his life. Travels on the Continent brought him into contact with Galileo, Mersenne and Gassendi, and a chance encounter with Euclid inspired his method. Fearing for his safety as the Civil War approached, he lived in Paris from 1640 to 1651, tutoring the future Charles II. He returned to England, survived accusations of atheism, and died aged ninety-one in 1679.

Hobbes held that everything is matter in motion, including thought and feeling. In Leviathan (1651) he argued that without government, human beings, roughly equal and driven by competition, diffidence and glory, would live in a war of every man against every man, in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Rational self-interest leads them to covenant to transfer their rights to a sovereign whose power must be undivided and absolute, limited only by the subject's right to preserve their life. His argument founded modern social contract theory, and its stark individualism shaped later debates from Locke and Rousseau to game theory.
portrait_file: Thomas Hobbes by John Michael Wright (colour) (3x4 cropped).jpg
portrait_caption: John Michael Wright, portrait of Thomas Hobbes, c. 1669–70, National Portrait Gallery, London

name: René Descartes
birthplace: La Haye en Touraine (now Descartes), France
bio: Often called the father of modern philosophy, Descartes sought certainty through methodical doubt, founded knowledge on 'I think, therefore I am', and divided reality into mind and matter.
bio_full: René Descartes was born in 1596 in La Haye in Touraine and educated by the Jesuits at La Flèche. After a law degree he joined the army of Maurice of Nassau and later served in Bavaria, where, on 10 November 1619, a day of meditation and three dreams convinced him of his mission to rebuild knowledge. From 1628 he lived in the Dutch Republic, moving frequently, and published the Discourse on Method (1637) with essays on optics, meteorology and geometry, the Meditations (1641) and the Principles of Philosophy (1644). In 1649 he accepted Queen Christina's invitation to Stockholm, where he died of pneumonia in February 1650.

In the Meditations Descartes doubts everything that can be doubted, even the existence of the physical world and the truths of mathematics, by imagining an evil deceiver. What survives is the certainty of his own existence as a thinking thing. From the idea of a perfect God he argues that God exists and is no deceiver, so that clear and distinct ideas can be trusted and the physical world, whose essence is extension, can be known mathematically. Mind and body are distinct substances, raising the problem of how they interact. He also invented analytic geometry. His project of rational foundations set the agenda for Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke and Kant, and his dualism remains the starting point of philosophy of mind.
portrait_file: Frans Hals - Portret van René Descartes.jpg
portrait_caption: After Frans Hals, portrait of René Descartes, c. 1649–1700, Louvre

name: Blaise Pascal
bio: Mathematician, physicist and Christian apologist, Pascal explored the limits of reason, human misery and greatness, and the famous Wager in his unfinished Pensées.
bio_full: Blaise Pascal was born in 1623 in Clermont in the Auvergne and educated by his father, a tax official with scientific interests. A prodigy, he wrote an essay on conic sections at sixteen, built one of the first mechanical calculators to help his father, carried out experiments on the vacuum and air pressure, and with Fermat laid the foundations of probability theory. His family came under the influence of Jansenism, a rigorous Augustinian movement within Catholicism, and after an intense religious experience on the night of 23 November 1654, recorded in his 'Memorial', he devoted himself to religion. His Provincial Letters (1656–57) satirised Jesuit moral theology. He died in Paris in 1662, aged thirty-nine.

The Pensées, notes for an unfinished defence of Christianity published after his death, portray human beings as both wretched and great: a 'thinking reed', fragile in a silent infinite universe yet aware of its fragility. We flee our condition through diversion. Reason cannot prove God, and 'the heart has its reasons which reason does not know'. The Wager argues that since reason cannot decide, a prudent person should stake their life on God's existence, where the possible gain is infinite. Pascal is read as a forerunner of existentialism and a master of French prose.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Blaise Pascal, anonymous, c. 1690, Palace of Versailles

name: Baruch Spinoza
bio: Spinoza identified God with Nature in a geometrically ordered system with one substance, and argued for freedom of thought and a secular reading of scripture.
bio_full: Baruch (later Benedictus) de Spinoza was born in 1632 into Amsterdam's community of Portuguese Jews, many of them descendants of forced converts who had fled the Iberian Inquisition. He studied in the community's schools and worked in the family import business. In 1656, aged twenty-three, he was expelled from the synagogue with an unusually harsh writ of excommunication, for reasons the writ does not specify. He lived modestly in Rijnsburg, Voorburg and The Hague, earning money partly by grinding lenses, corresponding with scientists and refusing a professorship at Heidelberg. His Theological-Political Treatise (1670) was published anonymously and banned. He died of a lung disease in 1677; the Ethics appeared after his death.

The Ethics, set out in the geometrical manner of definitions, axioms and propositions, argues that there is only one substance, God or Nature (Deus sive Natura), with infinite attributes, of which we know thought and extension; minds and bodies are two aspects of the same things. Everything follows from God's nature by necessity, so there is no free will in the usual sense and no purpose in nature. Freedom is understanding the causes of our emotions, and the highest happiness is the intellectual love of God. The Theological-Political Treatise defends freedom of thought and treats the Bible as a historical document. Reviled as an atheist for a century, he was rediscovered by Lessing, Goethe and the German idealists.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Baruch Spinoza, anonymous, c. 1665, Herzog August Bibliothek, Wolfenbüttel

name: John Locke
bio: Locke argued that all ideas come from experience and that legitimate government rests on consent and protects natural rights, laying foundations of empiricism and liberalism.
bio_full: John Locke was born in 1632 in Somerset to a Puritan family and studied at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, where he later taught and studied medicine. In 1667 he joined the household of Lord Ashley, later Earl of Shaftesbury, as physician and adviser, and became drawn into Whig opposition politics. Suspected of involvement in plots against Charles II and James II, he fled to the Netherlands in 1683. He returned after the Glorious Revolution of 1688–89 and quickly published the Essay Concerning Human Understanding, the Two Treatises of Government and A Letter Concerning Toleration. He spent his last years at Oates in Essex and died in 1704.

The Essay rejects innate ideas: the mind begins as 'white paper' and all ideas come from sensation and reflection. Locke distinguished primary qualities, such as shape and motion, from secondary qualities, such as colour, and made personal identity depend on continuity of consciousness rather than of substance. The Second Treatise argues that people in a state of nature have natural rights to life, liberty and property, which they acquire by mixing their labour with things, and that government exists by consent to protect those rights and may be resisted if it betrays its trust. His ideas shaped the Enlightenment and the American founders, while his own investments in colonial ventures and the slave trade are now part of the debate about his legacy.
portrait_file: Godfrey Kneller - Portrait of John Locke (Hermitage).jpg
portrait_caption: Godfrey Kneller, portrait of John Locke, 1697, Hermitage Museum

name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
bio: Polymath and co-inventor of the calculus, Leibniz pictured reality as countless simple substances, monads, in pre-established harmony, and held that this is the best of all possible worlds.
bio_full: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was born in Leipzig in 1646, the son of a professor of moral philosophy, and took a doctorate in law at Altdorf at twenty. He entered the service of the Elector of Mainz and spent 1672–76 in Paris on a diplomatic mission, where he studied mathematics with Christiaan Huygens and developed the calculus, independently of Newton; a bitter priority dispute followed. From 1676 until his death he served the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg in Hanover as librarian, historian and counsellor. He founded the Berlin Academy of Sciences, designed a calculating machine, worked on mining engineering and church reunion, and corresponded with hundreds of scholars. He died in Hanover in 1716, largely neglected.

Leibniz published only one philosophical book in his lifetime, the Theodicy (1710); most of his philosophy lies in essays and letters such as the Discourse on Metaphysics and the Monadology. Reality consists of monads, simple, unextended, soul-like substances, each mirroring the whole universe from its point of view. They do not interact; God has pre-established their harmony. Two great principles govern reasoning: non-contradiction and sufficient reason, that nothing happens without a reason. Since God chose freely among all possible worlds, this world must be the best possible, a view Voltaire mocked in Candide. His ideas on logic and a universal symbolic language anticipated modern logic and computing.
portrait_file: Christoph Bernhard Francke - Bildnis des Philosophen Leibniz (ca. 1695).jpg
portrait_caption: Christoph Bernhard Francke, portrait of Leibniz, c. 1695, Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, Braunschweig

name: Giambattista Vico
bio: Vico argued that we can truly know only what we have made, and so founded a 'new science' of history, myth and language against Descartes.
bio_full: Giambattista Vico was born in Naples in 1668, the son of a poor bookseller, and was largely self-taught after a childhood fall that kept him from school for years. He worked for nine years as a tutor at Vatolla in the Cilento, then in 1699 became professor of rhetoric at the University of Naples, a poorly paid post he held for over forty years. He failed to win the more prestigious chair of law in 1723. He published the first version of his New Science in 1725 and heavily revised editions in 1730 and 1744, the year he died.

Against Descartes, Vico held the principle verum ipsum factum: the true is what has been made, so that humans can have full knowledge of mathematics and of the civil world of nations, which they made, but not of nature, which God made. The New Science traces a recurring course through which nations pass, an age of gods, an age of heroes and an age of men, each with its own language, law and mentality, and interprets early myths and poetry as the 'poetic wisdom' of primitive peoples. Little read in his lifetime, he was rediscovered in the nineteenth century by Michelet, influenced Croce, Collingwood and Isaiah Berlin, and provided the structure of James Joyce's Finnegans Wake.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Giambattista Vico

name: George Berkeley
bio: Anglican bishop George Berkeley argued that there is no matter behind experience: to be is to be perceived, and the world exists as ideas in minds and in God.
bio_full: George Berkeley was born in 1685 near Kilkenny in Ireland and entered Trinity College, Dublin, at fifteen, becoming a fellow in 1707. In his twenties he published his main philosophical works: An Essay towards a New Theory of Vision (1709), A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous (1713). He travelled in Europe, became Dean of Derry and spent 1728–31 in Rhode Island waiting for promised funding for a college in Bermuda that never came; at his Rhode Island estate he owned enslaved people. He was Bishop of Cloyne from 1734 to 1752 and died in Oxford in 1753.

Berkeley argued that Locke's material substance, an unperceivable something underlying our ideas, is both unknowable and incoherent. The objects we perceive are collections of ideas, and their being is to be perceived (esse est percipi); minds, which perceive, are the only substances. Things continue to exist when no human perceives them because they are always perceived by God. He presented this immaterialism as the defence of common sense against scepticism and atheism. Samuel Johnson famously kicked a stone to 'refute' him, missing the point; Hume drew sceptical conclusions from his arguments, and he anticipated later phenomenalism.
portrait_file: John Smibert - Bishop George Berkeley - Google Art Project (cropped).jpg
portrait_caption: John Smibert, Bishop George Berkeley, c. 1727, National Portrait Gallery, London

name: Montesquieu
birthplace: Château de La Brède, near Bordeaux
bio: Montesquieu founded a comparative science of laws in The Spirit of the Laws and argued that political liberty depends on the separation of powers.
bio_full: Charles-Louis de Secondat, baron de La Brède et de Montesquieu, was born in 1689 at the Château de La Brède near Bordeaux. He studied law, inherited from his uncle the presidency of the Bordeaux parlement, and became a member of the Bordeaux academy. The Persian Letters (1721), a satire of French society seen through the eyes of two Persian travellers, made him famous. He sold his office, travelled through Europe from 1728 to 1731, and spent nearly two years in England, which he admired. He published Considerations on the Causes of the Greatness of the Romans and their Decline (1734) and, after twenty years' work, The Spirit of the Laws (1748). He died in Paris in 1755.

The Spirit of the Laws classifies governments as republics, monarchies and despotisms, each animated by its own principle, virtue, honour or fear, and argues that laws must suit a people's climate, geography, commerce, religion and customs. Its most famous chapter, drawn from an idealised picture of England, holds that liberty requires the legislative, executive and judicial powers to be held by different hands so that power checks power. The book was placed on the Catholic Index of forbidden books in 1751 but was cited more than any other modern source by the framers of the United States Constitution, and it is a founding text of comparative politics and sociology.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Montesquieu, anonymous, 18th century

name: Émilie du Châtelet
bio: Mathematician and natural philosopher, Émilie du Châtelet combined Newtonian physics with Leibnizian metaphysics and made the standard French translation of Newton's Principia.
bio_full: Gabrielle Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil was born in Paris in 1706 into an aristocratic family; her father encouraged her unusual education in languages and mathematics. At eighteen she married the marquis du Châtelet. From 1733 she lived with Voltaire, mainly at her husband's château at Cirey, where they built a library and laboratory and studied Newton together; she took lessons from the mathematicians Maupertuis and Clairaut. Her essay on the nature of fire was published by the Academy of Sciences in 1739. She died in 1749 at Lunéville, days after giving birth, having finished her translation of Newton.

In her Foundations of Physics (Institutions de physique, 1740) she argued that physics needs metaphysical foundations and drew on Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason while accepting Newton's mechanics, and defended a role for hypotheses in science. She took Leibniz's side against the Cartesians in the vis viva controversy, holding that the force of a moving body is proportional to mass times velocity squared, a precursor of the concept of kinetic energy. Her French translation of Newton's Principia with commentary, published in 1756–59, remains the standard French version. Long remembered mainly as Voltaire's companion, she is now recognised as a significant philosopher of science.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Émilie du Châtelet, after Maurice Quentin de La Tour

name: David Hume
bio: Hume showed that our beliefs about causation, the self and morality rest on custom and feeling rather than reason, and in doing so woke Kant from his 'dogmatic slumber'.
bio_full: David Hume was born in Edinburgh in 1711 and grew up at the family estate of Ninewells in Berwickshire. He entered Edinburgh University at about ten, tried law and commerce, and suffered a breakdown in his late teens. In France, at La Flèche, he wrote A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), which, he said, 'fell dead-born from the press'. Twice refused university chairs because of his reputation for irreligion, he worked as a tutor, secretary to a general, librarian of the Edinburgh Advocates' Library and diplomat in Paris, where the salons lionised him. His History of England made him famous and rich. He died in Edinburgh in 1776, calmly, as Adam Smith recorded.

Hume held that all ideas derive from impressions. We never perceive a necessary connection between cause and effect, only constant conjunction, and our expectation that the future will resemble the past rests on custom, not reason: the problem of induction. The self is nothing but a bundle of perceptions. Reason is the slave of the passions; morality is grounded in sentiment, and one cannot derive an 'ought' from an 'is'. His Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, published after his death, dismantled the argument from design, and his essay on miracles argued that testimony can never establish one. He is often counted the greatest philosopher to write in English.
portrait_caption: Allan Ramsay, portrait of David Hume, 1766, Scottish National Portrait Gallery

name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
bio: Rousseau argued that society corrupts naturally good human beings and, in The Social Contract, sought a legitimate state in which citizens obey a general will they themselves make.
bio_full: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712; his mother died days later, and he was raised by his father, a watchmaker, until he left the city at sixteen. Taken up by Madame de Warens in Savoy, he converted to Catholicism and educated himself. In Paris he befriended Diderot and wrote for the Encyclopédie. His prize-winning Discourse on the Sciences and Arts (1750) made him famous, followed by the Discourse on Inequality (1755), the novel Julie (1761), and in 1762 both Emile and The Social Contract, which were condemned in Paris and Geneva. He fled to Switzerland and England, quarrelled with Hume and most of his friends, and wrote the Confessions. He died at Ermenonville in 1778. He placed all five of his children with Thérèse Levasseur in a foundling hospital, a fact his critics never let him forget.

Rousseau held that human beings are naturally good, moved by self-love and pity, and that society, property and the desire for others' esteem (amour-propre) have produced inequality and dependence. The Social Contract opens with the claim that man is born free and everywhere is in chains, and seeks a form of association in which each, uniting with all, obeys only himself: sovereignty belongs to the general will, which aims at the common good. Emile set out an education following nature, and the Confessions founded modern autobiography. He inspired the French revolutionaries, Kant and the Romantics; critics have charged that his general will opens the way to coercion, a reading his defenders dispute.
