portrait_caption: Maurice Quentin de La Tour, portrait of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, 1753

name: Denis Diderot
bio: Chief editor of the Encyclopédie, Diderot developed a daring materialism of sensitive, self-organising matter, mostly in dialogues published after his death.
bio_full: Denis Diderot was born in 1713 in Langres, the son of a master cutler, and was educated by the Jesuits and in Paris, where he refused a settled profession and lived by translation and hack writing. His Letter on the Blind (1749), with its hints of atheism, earned him three months in prison at Vincennes. From 1747 he edited, with d'Alembert at first, the Encyclopédie, which survived censorship, suspension and the withdrawal of collaborators to reach seventeen volumes of text by 1765 and eleven of plates by 1772. He also wrote novels, plays and art criticism. In 1773–74 he visited Catherine the Great in St Petersburg; she had bought his library and appointed him its paid custodian. He died in Paris in 1784.

The Encyclopédie aimed to gather all knowledge, including the mechanical arts, and to 'change the common way of thinking', with cross-references used to slip past censors. Diderot's own philosophy, in works such as D'Alembert's Dream and Rameau's Nephew, which were published only after his death, imagines matter itself as capable of sensation, and life and thought as emerging from its organisation, an evolutionary materialism without God or fixed species. His dialogues stage unresolved arguments about morality, genius and social convention, and Hegel and Marx admired Rameau's Nephew.
portrait_file: Denis Diderot by Louis-Michel van Loo.jpg
portrait_caption: Louis-Michel van Loo, portrait of Denis Diderot, 1767, Louvre

name: Adam Smith
bio: Moral philosopher of the Scottish Enlightenment, Adam Smith grounded ethics in sympathy and the impartial spectator and founded modern economics with The Wealth of Nations.
bio_full: Adam Smith was born in Kirkcaldy, Fife, in 1723, a few months after his father's death. He studied at Glasgow under Francis Hutcheson and spent six years at Balliol College, Oxford, which he found intellectually idle. After lecturing in Edinburgh, he became professor of logic and then of moral philosophy at Glasgow in 1751–52. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) made his name, and in 1764 he resigned to tutor the young Duke of Buccleuch on a tour of France, where he met Quesnay and Turgot. He spent a decade writing The Wealth of Nations (1776), became Commissioner of Customs in Edinburgh, and died there in 1790. He was Hume's closest friend.

The Theory of Moral Sentiments explains moral judgment through sympathy, our capacity to imagine ourselves in another's situation, disciplined by the standpoint of an imagined impartial spectator, the 'man within the breast'. The Wealth of Nations argues that wealth arises from the division of labour and market exchange, criticises mercantilist restrictions, and describes how individuals pursuing their own gain are led, 'as by an invisible hand', to promote the public good. Smith also worried about the stultifying effects of repetitive labour and the collusion of merchants. Scholars debate how his two books fit together, the so-called 'Adam Smith problem', but most now see them as one moral and social science.
portrait_caption: The 'Muir portrait' of Adam Smith, anonymous, c. 1800

name: Immanuel Kant
bio: Kant argued that the mind structures experience through space, time and the categories, and that morality is a law rational beings give themselves; his critical philosophy reshaped every field of philosophy.
bio_full: Immanuel Kant was born in Königsberg in 1724, the son of a harness-maker, and raised in Pietism. He studied at the University of Königsberg, worked as a private tutor, and from 1755 lectured as a Privatdozent on logic, metaphysics, physics, geography and more. His early work included a theory of the origin of the solar system from a nebula. He became professor of logic and metaphysics in 1770, then spent eleven 'silent' years before publishing the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781. The next two decades produced the Groundwork (1785), the Critique of Practical Reason (1788), the Critique of Judgment (1790) and works on religion, politics and history; his book on religion brought a royal censure in 1794. He never travelled far from Königsberg and died there in 1804.

Kant described his 'Copernican revolution': instead of our knowledge conforming to objects, objects as we experience them conform to the forms of our sensibility, space and time, and the categories of the understanding, such as causality. This explains how synthetic knowledge a priori is possible, but limits knowledge to appearances; things in themselves, and God, freedom and immortality, lie beyond theoretical proof. In ethics, the categorical imperative commands us to act only on maxims we could will as universal laws and to treat humanity always as an end, never merely as a means. His aesthetics, his essay 'What is Enlightenment?' and his plan for perpetual peace remain foundational, and his philosophy launched German idealism.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Immanuel Kant, 18th century

name: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
bio: Dramatist and critic of the German Enlightenment, Lessing pleaded for religious toleration in Nathan the Wise and distinguished poetry from painting in Laocoön.
bio_full: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was born in Kamenz in Saxony in 1729, the son of a Lutheran pastor, and studied theology and medicine at Leipzig before turning to the theatre and journalism. In Berlin he became a close friend of the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn. He worked as secretary to a Prussian general in Breslau and as critic for the new Hamburg National Theatre, and from 1770 was librarian of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel. There he published fragments by the deist Hermann Samuel Reimarus attacking revealed religion, which drew him into a fierce controversy with the Hamburg pastor Goeze until the duke banned his theological writing. He died in Braunschweig in 1781.

Laocoön (1766) argued that painting and poetry have different laws, since painting represents bodies in space and poetry actions in time. In the theological controversy he insisted on an 'ugly broad ditch' between contingent historical truths and necessary truths of reason, so that faith cannot rest on historical proofs. Nathan the Wise (1779), whose hero was modelled on Mendelssohn, uses the parable of three rings to argue that Judaism, Christianity and Islam should prove their truth through love and conduct. The Education of the Human Race (1780) presents revelation as a stage in humanity's moral education. After his death Jacobi's report that Lessing had confessed to Spinozism set off the Pantheism Controversy.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, 18th century

name: Mary Wollstonecraft
bio: Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women's apparent inferiority is the product of denied education, founding modern feminist philosophy.
bio_full: Mary Wollstonecraft was born in London in 1759 into a family ruined by her father's drinking and violence. She worked as a lady's companion, ran a school at Newington Green with her sister and friend, where she met the Dissenting minister Richard Price, and served as a governess in Ireland. In London she became a reviewer and translator for the radical publisher Joseph Johnson. Her A Vindication of the Rights of Men (1790) answered Burke's attack on the French Revolution, and A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) followed. She lived in revolutionary Paris, had a daughter with the American Gilbert Imlay, and later married the philosopher William Godwin. She died in 1797 days after giving birth to their daughter, the future Mary Shelley.

Wollstonecraft argued that reason is the same in both sexes and that virtue, to be virtue at all, must be the free exercise of reason. Women seem frivolous and weak because they are educated only to please men, and both sexes are corrupted by a society built on rank and dependence. She called for coeducation, economic independence and, more cautiously, political representation for women. Godwin's candid memoir of her unconventional life damaged her reputation for a century, but she was rediscovered as the founding figure of liberal feminism.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Mary Wollstonecraft, late 18th century

name: Jeremy Bentham
bio: Bentham founded modern utilitarianism, judging every action and law by whether it promotes the greatest happiness, and devoted his life to legal and political reform.
bio_full: Jeremy Bentham was born in London in 1748, the son of a prosperous attorney, and was a precocious child who entered Oxford at twelve. He trained for the bar but, disgusted by the obscurity of English law, devoted himself instead to its reform. An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation was printed in 1780 and published in 1789. He spent years promoting the Panopticon, a circular prison in which inmates could always be watched, and the scheme's failure turned him toward democratic radicalism. With James Mill he led the 'philosophical radicals', and he helped found the Westminster Review. He died in 1832; at his wish his preserved skeleton, dressed and seated, the 'auto-icon', is displayed at University College London.

Bentham opened his Introduction by declaring that nature has placed mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. The principle of utility judges every action by its tendency to increase or diminish the happiness of those affected, and his 'felicific calculus' measured pleasures by intensity, duration, certainty, nearness and extent. He dismissed natural rights as 'nonsense upon stilts', argued for codified law, democratic suffrage, the decriminalisation of homosexuality and the protection of animals, whose capacity to suffer, he said, is what matters. John Stuart Mill refined his theory, and Foucault made the Panopticon an emblem of modern surveillance.
portrait_file: Jeremy Bentham by Henry William Pickersgill.jpg
portrait_caption: Henry William Pickersgill, portrait of Jeremy Bentham, 1829, National Portrait Gallery, London

name: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
bio: Fichte built the first post-Kantian idealist system, deriving all experience from the activity of a self-positing I, and was a founding figure of German nationalism.
bio_full: Johann Gottlieb Fichte was born in 1762 in Rammenau in Saxony to a family of ribbon weavers; a local nobleman paid for his schooling after being impressed by the boy. He studied theology at Jena and Leipzig and worked as a tutor. His Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation (1792), published anonymously, was at first taken for Kant's work, which made his reputation. He was appointed professor at Jena in 1794 but lost his post in 1799 in the 'atheism controversy'. In Berlin he wrote The Vocation of Man (1800) and, under French occupation, delivered the Addresses to the German Nation (1808). He became the first elected rector of the new University of Berlin and died there in 1814 of typhus caught from his wife, who had nursed wounded soldiers.

Fichte's Wissenschaftslehre, or Doctrine of Science, which he reworked many times, tries to derive Kant's forms of experience from a single first principle: the I posits itself, and in doing so posits a not-I that limits it. The world exists as the field for moral striving, and freedom is the root of both theory and practice. His Foundations of Natural Right (1796–97) argued that self-consciousness requires recognition by other free beings, an idea Hegel developed. His influence on Schelling and Hegel was decisive, while his nationalist Addresses had a troubled later history.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Johann Gottlieb Fichte, early 19th century

name: Friedrich Schleiermacher
bio: Theologian and philosopher, Schleiermacher made religion a matter of feeling, the feeling of absolute dependence, and founded modern hermeneutics as the general art of understanding.
bio_full: Friedrich Daniel Ernst Schleiermacher was born in 1768 in Breslau, the son of a Reformed army chaplain, and educated by the Moravian Brethren, whose piety marked him even after he lost his orthodox faith. He studied at Halle, became a preacher at the Charité hospital in Berlin and joined the Romantic circle of Friedrich Schlegel. On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers (1799) made him famous. He translated Plato into German, taught at Halle, and in 1810 helped found the University of Berlin, where he was professor of theology and preacher at Trinity Church until his death in 1834.

Schleiermacher argued that religion is neither metaphysics nor morality but a 'sense and taste for the infinite', later defined in The Christian Faith (1821–22) as the feeling of absolute dependence. His lectures on hermeneutics made interpretation a general art for any text, combining grammatical understanding of language with psychological understanding of the author, and stressed the circular relation between parts and whole. His lecture on translation distinguished bringing the author to the reader from bringing the reader to the author. He is regarded as the father of modern liberal Protestant theology, and Dilthey, Gadamer and Ricoeur built on his hermeneutics.
portrait_file: Portret van Friedrich Ernst Daniel Schleiermacher (cropped).jpg
portrait_caption: Printed portrait of Friedrich Schleiermacher, 19th century (Rijksmuseum)

name: G. W. F. Hegel
bio: Hegel described reality as spirit coming to know itself through history, conflict and reconciliation, in a system whose dialectical method shaped Marx and much of modern thought.
bio_full: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was born in Stuttgart in 1770 and studied theology at the Tübingen seminary, where he shared a room with Schelling and the poet Hölderlin and celebrated the French Revolution. After years as a house tutor he joined Schelling at Jena in 1801, and finished the Phenomenology of Spirit there in 1806 as Napoleon's army took the town. He then edited a newspaper in Bamberg, was headmaster of a gymnasium in Nuremberg, where he wrote the Science of Logic, and became professor at Heidelberg, where he published the Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences. From 1818 he held the chair of philosophy in Berlin, published the Philosophy of Right, and lectured on history, art, religion and the history of philosophy until he died in 1831, probably of cholera.

Hegel held that the real is rational and that reality as a whole, the Absolute, is spirit (Geist) developing through history toward self-knowledge and freedom. Thought proceeds dialectically: each position, pushed to its limits, reveals contradictions that are overcome and preserved in a richer standpoint. The Phenomenology traces consciousness through figures such as the master-slave dialectic, in which self-consciousness depends on recognition by another. His Philosophy of Right sees freedom realised in the family, civil society and the state. The 'thesis-antithesis-synthesis' formula is not his own. After his death his followers split into Right and Left Hegelians, and Marx, Kierkegaard, existentialism and critical theory all define themselves against him.
portrait_caption: Jakob Schlesinger, portrait of G. W. F. Hegel, 1831, Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin

name: Friedrich Schelling
bio: Schelling, the philosopher of Romantic nature, developed a philosophy of nature and of identity, a celebrated essay on human freedom, and a late 'positive philosophy' that challenged Hegel.
bio_full: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling was born in 1775 in Leonberg, Württemberg, and entered the Tübingen seminary at fifteen, sharing rooms with Hegel and Hölderlin. A prodigy, he was appointed professor at Jena in 1798, aged twenty-three, at the centre of the Romantic circle; he married Caroline Schlegel. He later taught at Würzburg and Erlangen and worked in Munich, where he published Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom in 1809, his last major work printed in his lifetime. In 1841 he was called to Berlin to combat Hegelianism, and his lectures were attended by Kierkegaard, Engels and Bakunin. He died in Switzerland in 1854.

Schelling began as a follower of Fichte but argued that nature is not merely the not-I but visible spirit, a self-organising whole in which mind slumbers; his System of Transcendental Idealism (1800) made art the highest organ of philosophy. His identity philosophy treated nature and spirit as expressions of one absolute, which Hegel mocked in the Phenomenology's preface. The freedom essay locates the possibility of evil in a dark ground within God, and the late 'positive philosophy' insisted that reason cannot explain why anything exists at all. Long overshadowed by Hegel, he is now read as an ancestor of existentialism and environmental philosophy.
portrait_file: Nb pinacoteca stieler friedrich wilhelm joseph von schelling.jpg
portrait_caption: Joseph Karl Stieler, portrait of Friedrich Schelling, 1835, Neue Pinakothek, Munich

name: Arthur Schopenhauer
bio: Schopenhauer taught that the inner nature of the world is a blind, striving will, that life is therefore suffering, and that release comes through art, compassion and renunciation.
bio_full: Arthur Schopenhauer was born in Danzig in 1788 to a wealthy merchant family that moved to Hamburg in 1793. After his father's probable suicide in 1805 he abandoned a commercial career, studied at Göttingen and Berlin, and wrote a doctoral thesis on the principle of sufficient reason. His mother, the novelist Johanna Schopenhauer, ran a salon in Weimar where he met Goethe; the two quarrelled bitterly and became estranged. His main work, The World as Will and Representation, appeared in December 1818 dated 1819, and was ignored. He scheduled his Berlin lectures at the same hour as Hegel's and drew almost no students. He settled in Frankfurt in 1833, living on his inheritance, and found fame only in the 1850s after Parerga and Paralipomena (1851). He died in 1860.

Schopenhauer accepted Kant's distinction between appearance and thing in itself, but argued that we know the thing in itself from within as will: a blind, aimless striving that manifests itself in all of nature, from gravity to human desire. Because will is never satisfied, life oscillates between pain and boredom. Relief comes in aesthetic contemplation, above all of music, which he saw as a direct copy of the will; in compassion, the basis of morality; and in ascetic denial of the will, which he compared to Buddhist and Hindu teaching. He was among the first Western philosophers to engage seriously with Indian thought, and he deeply influenced Wagner, Nietzsche, Freud, Tolstoy and the young Wittgenstein.
portrait_file: Arthur Schopenhauer Portrait by Ludwig Sigismund Ruhl 1815.jpeg
portrait_caption: Ludwig Sigismund Ruhl, portrait of Arthur Schopenhauer, 1815

name: Auguste Comte
bio: Comte founded positivism, held that thought passes through theological, metaphysical and scientific stages, and coined the word 'sociology'.
bio_full: Isidore Auguste Marie François Xavier Comte was born in Montpellier in 1798 into a Catholic and royalist family. He studied at the École Polytechnique in Paris, which was closed in 1816, and became secretary to the social theorist Henri de Saint-Simon before a bitter break in 1824. He suffered a mental breakdown in 1826 but went on to publish the six-volume Course of Positive Philosophy (1830–42), supporting himself as a tutor and examiner. After the death of Clotilde de Vaux in 1846, whom he loved, he turned to founding a Religion of Humanity, set out in the System of Positive Polity (1851–54). He died in Paris in 1857.

Comte's law of three stages holds that each branch of knowledge passes from a theological stage, explaining by gods, through a metaphysical stage, explaining by abstract forces, to a positive stage that seeks only laws linking observable phenomena. The sciences form a hierarchy from mathematics through astronomy, physics, chemistry and biology to sociology, the science of society, which he named and placed at the summit. His later Religion of Humanity, with its calendar of secular saints, was mocked by John Stuart Mill, who had admired his earlier work. Positivism shaped nineteenth-century social science, and the motto 'Order and Progress' on Brazil's flag is his.
portrait_file: Portrait of Auguste Comte by Antoine Étex.jpg
portrait_caption: Antoine Étex, portrait of Auguste Comte

name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
bio: Essayist and lecturer, Ralph Waldo Emerson led American Transcendentalism and preached self-reliance, intellectual independence and the divinity of nature.
bio_full: Ralph Waldo Emerson was born in Boston in 1803, the son of a Unitarian minister who died when he was eight. He graduated from Harvard and became a Unitarian minister himself, but after the death of his young wife Ellen he resigned his pulpit in 1832, unable to administer communion in good conscience. A trip to Europe brought him into contact with Coleridge, Wordsworth and Carlyle. Settling in Concord, Massachusetts, he published Nature in 1836, and his 'American Scholar' address (1837) and 'Divinity School Address' (1838), which scandalised Harvard. He earned his living as a lecturer for decades, published Essays (1841, 1844), supported abolition, and died in Concord in 1882.

Emerson held that each individual has direct access to truth and the divine through intuition, without the mediation of churches or traditions: 'Trust thyself' is the message of 'Self-Reliance'. Nature is a symbol of spirit, and the universal 'Over-Soul' unites all beings. He drew on Plato, Kant as filtered through Coleridge, and Hindu scriptures. His call for an original American culture shaped Thoreau, Whitman, Dickinson and William James, and Nietzsche read him with admiration.

name: Henry David Thoreau
bio: Henry David Thoreau tested Transcendentalism by living simply at Walden Pond and defended the individual conscience against unjust government in 'Civil Disobedience'.
bio_full: Henry David Thoreau was born in Concord in 1817 and studied at Harvard. He taught school, worked in his family's pencil business and as a surveyor, and became a friend and sometime lodger of Emerson. From July 1845 to September 1847 he lived in a cabin he built on Emerson's land at Walden Pond. In 1846 he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay his poll tax in protest against slavery and the Mexican War, the origin of his lecture 'Resistance to Civil Government' (1849), later known as 'Civil Disobedience'. Walden appeared in 1854. He defended John Brown after the raid on Harpers Ferry and died of tuberculosis in 1862.

Walden is both a record of an experiment in deliberate living and a philosophical argument that most people lead lives of quiet desperation, enslaved by possessions and opinion. Nature, attended to closely, is a source of moral and spiritual renewal. 'Civil Disobedience' argues that individuals must not lend themselves to the wrong they condemn and may break unjust laws openly, accepting the penalty. Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. drew on the essay, and Thoreau's journals and natural history writing made him a founding figure of environmentalism.
portrait_file: Bust of Thoreau by Walton Ricketson.jpg
portrait_caption: Walton Ricketson, bust of Henry David Thoreau

name: Alexis de Tocqueville
bio: In Democracy in America, Alexis de Tocqueville analysed how equality transforms politics and character, warning of the tyranny of the majority and a mild 'soft despotism'.
bio_full: Alexis de Tocqueville was born in Paris in 1805 into an aristocratic Norman family; several relatives had been guillotined in the Revolution and his parents had narrowly escaped. Trained as a lawyer, he travelled through the United States in 1831–32 with his friend Gustave de Beaumont, officially to study prisons. The two volumes of Democracy in America (1835, 1840) made him famous. He was elected to the Chamber of Deputies, wrote on Algeria, and after the 1848 revolution helped draft the constitution of the Second Republic and served briefly as foreign minister. Opposing Louis-Napoleon's coup in 1851, he withdrew from politics and wrote The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856). He died of tuberculosis in 1859.

Tocqueville argued that the advance of 'equality of conditions' is irresistible across the Christian world, and that America showed both its promise and its dangers. Democratic peoples may suffer a tyranny of the majority over thought itself, and individualism may lead them to withdraw into private life, leaving an immense tutelary power to manage them gently: a soft despotism. The antidotes are local self-government, free associations, a free press, religion and the mores of citizens. In The Old Regime he argued that the Revolution continued the centralisation of the monarchy. He is a founder of political sociology and a central figure for liberals and conservatives alike.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Alexis de Tocqueville, 19th century

name: John Stuart Mill
bio: John Stuart Mill refined utilitarianism with higher and lower pleasures and, in On Liberty, defended individual freedom through the harm principle; he was the most influential English philosopher of his century.
bio_full: John Stuart Mill was born in London in 1806, the son of the philosopher James Mill, who educated him at home in a famously rigorous programme: Greek at three, Latin at eight, logic and political economy by his early teens, as a future leader of Bentham's utilitarian radicals. At twenty he suffered a mental crisis, which he overcame partly through Wordsworth's poetry. He worked for the East India Company from 1823 to 1858. In 1830 he met Harriet Taylor, whom he married in 1851 after her husband's death and credited as co-author of much of his work. He published A System of Logic (1843), Principles of Political Economy (1848), On Liberty (1859), Utilitarianism (1861) and The Subjection of Women (1869), and served as a Member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868. He died in Avignon in 1873.

Mill defended Bentham's principle of utility but argued that some pleasures, those of the intellect, feeling and imagination, are higher in quality: better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. On Liberty holds that the only purpose for which power can rightly be exercised over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others, and that free discussion is necessary even for true opinions to remain alive. His Logic developed methods of inductive inference, and The Subjection of Women argued for full legal and political equality of the sexes. In Parliament he proposed votes for women. He remains the central figure of classical liberalism.
portrait_caption: George Frederic Watts, portrait of John Stuart Mill, 1873

name: Harriet Taylor Mill
bio: Harriet Taylor Mill wrote 'The Enfranchisement of Women' and was John Stuart Mill's intellectual partner, pushing liberalism toward full equality of the sexes.
bio_full: Harriet Hardy was born in London in 1807 and married the merchant John Taylor at eighteen. In 1830 she met John Stuart Mill, and for two decades the two maintained an intense intellectual friendship that scandalised their circle, while she remained married to Taylor. After Taylor's death they married in 1851. She suffered from tuberculosis and died in Avignon in 1858, where Mill bought a house overlooking her grave.

Her essay 'The Enfranchisement of Women' (1851), published under Mill's name in the Westminster Review, demanded equal education, employment, political rights and partnership in marriage. Mill credited her as joint author of On Liberty and as a decisive influence on the Principles of Political Economy and The Subjection of Women. The extent of her contribution was long dismissed, but recent scholarship has taken her claims and her own writings on marriage, divorce and toleration seriously, while still debating the precise division of labour.
portrait_caption: Portrait of Harriet Taylor Mill, c. 1834, National Portrait Gallery, London

name: Søren Kierkegaard
bio: Søren Kierkegaard re-centred philosophy on the single existing individual, on choice, anxiety, despair and faith, against Hegel's system and Denmark's complacent Christianity.
bio_full: Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813, the youngest child of a wealthy, melancholy and devout hosier. He studied theology at the University of Copenhagen and wrote a dissertation on irony. In 1840 he became engaged to Regine Olsen but broke the engagement the following year, an event that haunted his writing. From 1843 he published a stream of works, many under pseudonyms, including Either/Or, Fear and Trembling, The Concept of Anxiety, Concluding Unscientific Postscript and The Sickness unto Death. He was mocked in the satirical paper The Corsair, and in his last year he attacked the Danish state church in pamphlets. He collapsed in the street and died in 1855.

Kierkegaard held that truth for an existing person is subjectivity: what matters is not objective knowledge but how one relates to what one believes. Life can be lived in the aesthetic sphere of pleasure and possibility, the ethical sphere of duty and commitment, or the religious sphere of faith, and the move between them is a leap, not a logical step. Fear and Trembling uses Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac to probe a faith that goes beyond ethics. Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom, and despair is the failure to be oneself before God. Rediscovered in the twentieth century, he became a founding source for existentialism and modern theology; his pseudonyms mean that attributing views to him directly requires care.
portrait_caption: Sketch of Søren Kierkegaard by his cousin Niels Christian Kierkegaard, c. 1840

name: Ludwig Feuerbach
bio: A leading Young Hegelian, Ludwig Feuerbach argued that God is humanity's projection of its own essence, an idea that shaped Marx.
bio_full: Ludwig Feuerbach was born in Landshut, Bavaria, in 1804, the son of a distinguished jurist. He studied theology at Heidelberg and then philosophy under Hegel in Berlin. His anonymous Thoughts on Death and Immortality (1830), which denied personal immortality, ended his academic career. He lived for many years in rural Bruckberg, supported by his wife's share in a porcelain factory, and wrote The Essence of Christianity (1841), translated into English by George Eliot. After the factory failed he lived in poverty and died near Nuremberg in 1872.

Feuerbach argued that theology is really anthropology: the attributes humans ascribe to God, love, wisdom, justice, are the qualities of the human species, projected outward and alienated. Religion impoverishes human beings by locating their best powers in another being, and philosophy must restore them. He also inverted Hegel by insisting that sensuous, embodied human beings, not abstract spirit, are the starting point. Marx and Engels were briefly 'Feuerbachians', and Marx's 'Theses on Feuerbach' (1845) criticised him for failing to see that the world must be changed, not only interpreted.

name: Max Stirner
bio: In The Ego and Its Own, Max Stirner attacked every abstraction set above the individual, God, humanity, the state, morality, as a 'spook'.
bio_full: Max Stirner was the pen name of Johann Kaspar Schmidt, born in Bayreuth in 1806. He studied in Berlin, where he heard Hegel, and worked as a teacher at a girls' school while frequenting the Young Hegelian circle known as 'the Free' at Hippel's wine bar. The Ego and Its Own appeared in 1844 (dated 1845) and caused a brief sensation. A dairy business failed, he was twice imprisoned for debt, and he died in obscurity in Berlin in 1856.

Stirner turned the Young Hegelian critique of religion against the critics themselves: Feuerbach's 'humanity', the liberals' state, the socialists' society and morality itself are just new sacred ideas, 'spooks' or 'fixed ideas', to which the individual is sacrificed. Only the unique one, who owns himself and treats everything as his property, is real; in place of the state he imagined a 'union of egoists'. Marx and Engels devoted much of The German Ideology to attacking him. He was rediscovered in the 1890s and became a reference point for individualist anarchism, and some scholars see him as an anticipator of Nietzsche and post-structuralism.

name: Karl Marx
bio: Karl Marx analysed capitalism as a historically specific system built on the exploitation of wage labour, and history as shaped by modes of production and class struggle.
bio_full: Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818 into a family of Jewish descent; his father had converted to Lutheranism to continue practising law. He studied law and philosophy in Bonn and Berlin, joined the Young Hegelians, and took a doctorate on Democritus and Epicurus. Barred from an academic career, he edited the Rheinische Zeitung until it was suppressed in 1843, then moved to Paris, where he began his lifelong partnership with Friedrich Engels, and to Brussels, where they wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848). After the 1848 revolutions he settled in London, where he lived in poverty, supported by Engels and by journalism, studied in the British Museum Reading Room, and helped lead the International Working Men's Association. Volume one of Capital appeared in 1867. He died in London in 1883.

Marx's historical materialism holds that the way societies produce their material life shapes their politics, law and ideas, and that history moves through conflicts between classes. Under capitalism, workers sell their labour power and produce more value than they are paid, the surplus value that is the source of profit; capitalism's dynamism also generates crises and, he predicted, its own overthrow by the proletariat. His early manuscripts analyse the alienation of workers from their labour, its products and one another. Whether the young humanist and the mature economist are one thinker is a long-running debate. His ideas shaped the labour movement, twentieth-century communist states and much of modern social science.

name: Franz Brentano
bio: Franz Brentano revived the scholastic idea of intentionality, the 'aboutness' of the mental, and taught a generation that included Husserl and Freud.
bio_full: Franz Clemens Brentano was born in 1838 at Marienberg on the Rhine into a distinguished Catholic family; the Romantic writers Clemens Brentano and Bettina von Arnim were his uncle and aunt. He studied philosophy, wrote a dissertation on the senses of being in Aristotle, and was ordained a priest in 1864. He taught at Würzburg, but his opposition to the new dogma of papal infallibility led him to leave the priesthood in 1873. He became professor at Vienna in 1874, the year Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint appeared, but had to give up his chair to marry, since Austrian law treated him as still a priest. He continued teaching as a lecturer, moved to Florence and then Zürich, went blind, and died in 1917.

Brentano argued that what distinguishes mental from physical phenomena is intentionality: every mental act is directed at an object, as hearing is of a sound and wishing is for something. He classified mental acts into presentations, judgments and acts of love and hate, and developed a theory of value based on correct emotions. His greatest influence came through students: Husserl, Meinong, Twardowski, Stumpf and Christian von Ehrenfels, while Freud attended his lectures. Phenomenology, the Austrian theory of objects and the Polish school of logic all trace back to him.

name: Henry Sidgwick
bio: In The Methods of Ethics, Henry Sidgwick gave classical utilitarianism its most rigorous statement, ending honestly in an unresolved 'dualism of practical reason'.
bio_full: Henry Sidgwick was born in 1838 in Skipton, Yorkshire, the son of a clergyman schoolmaster, and studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow. In 1869 he resigned his fellowship because he could no longer subscribe in conscience to the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England, an act that helped end religious tests at the universities. He became Knightbridge Professor of Moral Philosophy in 1883. With his wife Eleanor Balfour he helped found Newnham College for women, and he was the first president of the Society for Psychical Research. He died in 1900.

The Methods of Ethics (1874) compares three methods of deciding what we ought to do: egoism, intuitionism and utilitarianism. Sidgwick argued that the intuitions of common-sense morality are best systematised by utilitarianism, grounded in self-evident axioms of impartiality and benevolence, but he could find no rational way to settle the conflict between one's own good and the universal good: the dualism of practical reason. Admired by Rawls, Parfit and Singer as the most careful work of classical ethics, the book shaped twentieth-century analytic moral philosophy.

name: Charles Sanders Peirce
bio: Founder of pragmatism and a pioneer of logic and the theory of signs, Charles Sanders Peirce held that truth is what inquiry would ultimately converge on.
bio_full: Charles Sanders Peirce was born in 1839 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the son of the Harvard mathematician Benjamin Peirce. He studied chemistry at Harvard and worked for thirty years as a scientist for the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey, making important measurements of gravity. With William James and others he formed the informal 'Metaphysical Club' in Cambridge in the early 1870s. He lectured on logic at Johns Hopkins from 1879 to 1884 but was dismissed, apparently in part because of scandal about his divorce and remarriage, and never held another academic post. He spent his last decades in poverty in Milford, Pennsylvania, writing thousands of pages that remained unpublished at his death in 1914.

In 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear' (1878) Peirce stated the pragmatic maxim: our conception of an object is our conception of its conceivable practical effects. Inquiry begins with doubt and aims at settled belief, and truth is the opinion that the community of investigators is fated to reach in the long run; all our knowledge is fallible. He developed a logic of relations and quantification independently of Frege, a classification of signs into icons, indices and symbols that founded semiotics, and the idea of abduction, inference to an explanatory hypothesis. Disliking James's version of pragmatism, he renamed his own 'pragmaticism'.

name: William James
bio: Psychologist and philosopher William James made pragmatism a public philosophy, defended the will to believe, and described the stream of consciousness.
bio_full: William James was born in New York City in 1842, the eldest son of the theologian Henry James Sr. and brother of the novelist Henry James. He had an unsettled cosmopolitan education in Europe, studied painting, then chemistry and medicine at Harvard, and joined Louis Agassiz's expedition to Brazil. After a period of depression in his twenties, he began teaching at Harvard in 1872, first physiology, then psychology, then philosophy. The Principles of Psychology (1890) took twelve years to write. Later came The Will to Believe (1897), The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) and Pragmatism (1907). He died in New Hampshire in 1910.

James defined truth pragmatically: true ideas are those we can assimilate, validate and verify, that 'work' in the long run of experience. 'The Will to Believe' argues that where evidence cannot decide a live, forced and momentous option, such as religious belief, we have the right to believe. The Principles described consciousness as a stream and proposed the James-Lange theory of emotion. His 'radical empiricism' held that relations are as directly experienced as things. A pluralist and anti-absolutist, he influenced Dewey, Husserl, Bergson and Wittgenstein.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
bio: Nietzsche diagnosed the collapse of Christian values, 'God is dead', and called for the creation of new values through genealogy, self-overcoming and the affirmation of life.
bio_full: Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born in 1844 in Röcken, near Leipzig, the son of a Lutheran pastor who died when he was four. A brilliant student of classical philology at Bonn and Leipzig, he was appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, before completing his doctorate. He became a close friend of Richard Wagner and published The Birth of Tragedy (1872), but later broke with Wagner. Ill health forced him to resign in 1879, and for the next decade he lived a wandering life in Switzerland and Italy on a small pension, writing Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, On the Genealogy of Morality and other works. In January 1889 he suffered a mental collapse in Turin and never recovered; he died in Weimar in 1900. His sister Elisabeth, who controlled his papers, distorted his work and promoted it to German nationalists and later the Nazis.

Nietzsche argued that the 'death of God', the loss of belief in Christianity, leaves European culture facing nihilism, because its values rested on that belief. His genealogy traces morality to its origins, arguing that Christian 'slave morality' arose from the resentment of the weak against the noble. He proposed instead the affirmation of life, tested by the thought of the eternal recurrence of all things, the figure of the Übermensch who creates values, and the will to power as a basic drive. He wrote in aphorisms and was suspicious of systems. He became a central source for existentialism, psychoanalysis and post-structuralism; his appropriation by the Nazis rested heavily on his sister's editing, and he had repeatedly denounced the antisemites of his day.
