name: Gottlob Frege
bio: Gottlob Frege invented modern predicate logic, distinguished the sense of an expression from its reference, and tried to found arithmetic on logic alone.
bio_full: Friedrich Ludwig Gottlob Frege was born in Wismar on the Baltic coast in 1848 and studied mathematics, physics and philosophy at Jena and Göttingen. He spent his entire career teaching mathematics at Jena, little recognised outside a small circle. His Begriffsschrift (1879) introduced a formal logical language; The Foundations of Arithmetic (1884) followed, and the first volume of Basic Laws of Arithmetic appeared in 1893. In 1902, as the second volume was in press, Bertrand Russell wrote to tell him that his system allowed a contradiction. He retired in 1918 and died in 1925. His late diaries contain antisemitic and nationalist views that have troubled his admirers.

The Begriffsschrift gave logic quantifiers and variables, making it possible to analyse the structure of mathematical reasoning for the first time and laying the groundwork for modern logic and computer science. In 'On Sense and Reference' (1892) he explained how 'the morning star is the evening star' can be informative: the two names share a reference but differ in sense, the mode of presentation. His logicism, the project of deriving arithmetic from logic, foundered on Russell's paradox. Through Russell, Wittgenstein and Carnap he became the founding figure of analytic philosophy and the philosophy of language.

name: John Dewey
bio: John Dewey rebuilt philosophy around experience and inquiry and turned pragmatism into the most influential philosophy of education and democracy of his century.
bio_full: John Dewey was born in Burlington, Vermont, in 1859 and took a doctorate at Johns Hopkins, where he studied with Peirce and was drawn to Hegel. He taught at Michigan and from 1894 at the University of Chicago, where he founded the Laboratory School to test his educational ideas. In 1904 he moved to Columbia University in New York, where he taught until 1930. He lectured in Japan and China in 1919–21, helped found the American Association of University Professors and the American Civil Liberties Union, and in 1937 chaired the commission that examined the Moscow Trials' charges against Trotsky. He wrote about forty books and died in New York in 1952.

Dewey held that thought is an instrument for solving problems in experience, and that inquiry, the transformation of an unsettled situation into a settled one, is the model for all knowing. He rejected the dualisms of mind and body, theory and practice, and fact and value. In Democracy and Education (1916) he argued that education is growth, best achieved through active, social learning, and that democracy is not just a form of government but a way of associated living. His influence on education worldwide was immense, and Richard Rorty and others revived his pragmatism in the late twentieth century.

name: Edmund Husserl
bio: Edmund Husserl founded phenomenology, a method for describing experience exactly as it is lived, captured in the slogan 'back to the things themselves'.
bio_full: Edmund Husserl was born in 1859 into a Jewish family in Prossnitz, Moravia, and studied mathematics in Leipzig, Berlin and Vienna, where Brentano's lectures turned him to philosophy. He converted to Lutheranism in 1886. He taught at Halle, Göttingen and from 1916 Freiburg, where Heidegger became his assistant and successor. His Logical Investigations (1900–01) launched phenomenology, and Ideas I (1913) gave it a transcendental turn. After his retirement the Nazi regime stripped him of his rights as a Jew, and Heidegger, as rector, did nothing to help. He died in Freiburg in 1938. A Franciscan priest, Herman Van Breda, smuggled his forty thousand pages of shorthand manuscripts to Leuven, where the Husserl Archives still edit them.

Husserl held that philosophy must begin from careful description of conscious experience. By the epoché, or 'bracketing', we suspend the natural assumption that the world exists independently and attend to how things are given to consciousness. Consciousness is always intentional, of something, and its acts and their objects can be analysed with rigour. In his late Crisis of European Sciences he argued that the mathematical sciences have forgotten their roots in the 'lifeworld' of everyday experience. Heidegger, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty, Levinas and Derrida all began from his work.

name: Henri Bergson
bio: Henri Bergson contrasted lived time, duration, with the spatialised time of clocks and science, and described evolution as driven by a creative élan vital.
bio_full: Henri Bergson was born in Paris in 1859 to a Polish-Jewish composer and an English mother. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure, taught at lycées, and published Time and Free Will (1889) and Matter and Memory (1896). He became professor at the Collège de France in 1900, where his lectures drew crowds so large they became a society event. Creative Evolution (1907) made him the most famous philosopher in the world, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927. He served on diplomatic missions during the First World War and chaired the League of Nations committee on intellectual cooperation. He died in occupied Paris in January 1941.

Bergson argued that the intellect, made for acting on matter, cuts reality into static units, and so misses duration (la durée), the indivisible flow of lived time in which past and present interpenetrate. Intuition, a kind of intellectual sympathy, can grasp it. Memory is not stored in the brain but is the survival of the past in consciousness. Evolution is not mechanical but driven by an élan vital, a creative impulse. His popularity faded after the 1920s, but he influenced Proust, William James, Whitehead, Merleau-Ponty and, decisively, Gilles Deleuze.

name: Alfred North Whitehead
bio: Mathematician turned metaphysician, Alfred North Whitehead co-wrote Principia Mathematica with Russell and then built a philosophy of process in Process and Reality.
bio_full: Alfred North Whitehead was born in Ramsgate, Kent, in 1861, the son of a clergyman schoolmaster, and studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he became a fellow and taught Bertrand Russell. Together they wrote the three volumes of Principia Mathematica (1910–13). He moved to University College London and Imperial College, writing on the philosophy of science, and in 1924, aged sixty-three, accepted a chair of philosophy at Harvard. There he wrote Science and the Modern World (1925), Process and Reality (1929) and Adventures of Ideas (1933). He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1947.

Whitehead argued that modern science committed the 'fallacy of misplaced concreteness', taking abstractions such as bits of matter at an instant for concrete reality. Process and Reality describes the world as made of 'actual occasions', momentary events of experience that come into being by taking up, or 'prehending', their past and then perish into the future; God is the ground of novelty and order in this process. His remark that European philosophy consists of footnotes to Plato is often quoted. His metaphysics was largely neglected by analytic philosophy but founded process theology and influenced environmental philosophy and Susanne Langer.

name: Bertrand Russell
bio: Logician, philosopher and public intellectual, Bertrand Russell discovered Russell's paradox, developed the theory of descriptions and helped found analytic philosophy.
bio_full: Bertrand Arthur William Russell was born in 1872 into an aristocratic Whig family; his grandfather had twice been prime minister. Orphaned young, he was raised by his grandmother at Pembroke Lodge in Richmond. He studied mathematics and philosophy at Trinity College, Cambridge, and with G. E. Moore rebelled against British idealism. He wrote The Principles of Mathematics (1903) and, with Whitehead, Principia Mathematica, and taught Wittgenstein. His pacifism in the First World War cost him his Cambridge lectureship and six months in prison. He married four times, founded an experimental school, wrote prolifically on politics, religion, education and marriage, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950, and led the campaign for nuclear disarmament. He died in Wales in 1970, aged ninety-seven.

Russell's paradox, concerning the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, showed that Frege's logic was inconsistent, and his theory of types was one response. His theory of descriptions (1905) analysed phrases such as 'the present King of France' so that sentences about non-existent things are meaningful but false, a model of philosophical analysis. He developed logical atomism and theories of knowledge by acquaintance and description. His Problems of Philosophy (1912) and History of Western Philosophy (1945) made philosophy accessible to millions.

name: G. E. Moore
bio: G. E. Moore defended common sense against scepticism and idealism and, in Principia Ethica, argued that 'good' cannot be defined, coining the 'naturalistic fallacy'.
bio_full: George Edward Moore was born in 1873 in Upper Norwood, London, and studied classics and then philosophy at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he was elected to the Apostles discussion society. With Russell he broke from the dominant Hegelian idealism around 1898. Principia Ethica (1903) became the bible of the Bloomsbury Group, several of whose members had been fellow Apostles. He taught at Cambridge from 1911, held the chair of philosophy from 1925 to 1939, and edited the journal Mind from 1921 to 1947. He died in Cambridge in 1958.

Principia Ethica argued that goodness is a simple, non-natural property that cannot be defined; any attempt to identify it with a natural property such as pleasure commits the naturalistic fallacy, as shown by the 'open question' whether pleasure is good. The most valuable things are personal affection and the enjoyment of beauty. In epistemology, 'A Defence of Common Sense' (1925) and 'Proof of an External World' (1939), with its 'Here is one hand', held that we know many ordinary truths more certainly than any philosophical argument against them. Moore's paradox about saying 'it is raining but I don't believe it' fascinated Wittgenstein.

name: Karl Jaspers
bio: Psychiatrist turned philosopher, Karl Jaspers wrote of boundary situations, the Axial Age and German guilt, and was a founder of existential philosophy.
bio_full: Karl Jaspers was born in Oldenburg in 1883 and studied law and then medicine. He worked at the psychiatric clinic in Heidelberg and published General Psychopathology (1913), a landmark of psychiatry. He then turned to philosophy, becoming professor at Heidelberg in 1921; Philosophy appeared in three volumes in 1932. Married to Gertrud Mayer, who was Jewish, he was removed from his post in 1937, and the couple kept cyanide ready in case of deportation, which was reportedly scheduled shortly before American troops reached Heidelberg in 1945. After the war he wrote The Question of German Guilt (1946) and The Origin and Goal of History (1949). He moved to Basel in 1948 and died there in 1969. He was Hannah Arendt's doctoral supervisor and lifelong friend.

Jaspers held that the deepest truths of human existence are revealed in boundary situations, such as death, suffering, struggle and guilt, which cannot be changed or escaped and which shatter ordinary security. Being as a whole, 'the Encompassing', cannot be an object of knowledge, but is approached through 'ciphers' and philosophical faith. He coined the term Axial Age for the period around 800–200 BC when the great traditions of China, India, Persia, Israel and Greece emerged. The German Guilt book distinguished criminal, political, moral and metaphysical guilt.

name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
bio: Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote two philosophies: the Tractatus, with its picture theory of meaning, and the Philosophical Investigations, which repudiated it in favour of meaning as use.
bio_full: Ludwig Josef Johann Wittgenstein was born in Vienna in 1889, the youngest child of the steel magnate Karl Wittgenstein, in one of the richest families in Europe. He studied engineering in Berlin and Manchester before going to Cambridge in 1911 to work with Russell on logic. He served in the Austrian army in the First World War, finishing the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (published 1921–22), and then gave away his fortune and worked as a primary schoolteacher in rural Austria, a gardener and an architect. He returned to Cambridge in 1929, became professor in 1939, and worked as a hospital porter in London during the Second World War. He resigned in 1947, spent time in Ireland, and died in Cambridge in 1951. The Philosophical Investigations appeared posthumously in 1953.

The Tractatus holds that language pictures possible facts, that logical propositions are tautologies, and that ethics, aesthetics and the meaning of life cannot be said but only shown: 'whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent'. The Vienna Circle read it as a positivist manifesto, which he resisted. The later work treats meaning as use within 'language-games' embedded in forms of life, explains general terms by family resemblance, and argues that a purely private language is impossible; philosophical problems arise when language 'goes on holiday'. How sharply the two philosophies differ is debated. This section has separate entries on the early and late Wittgenstein.

name: Martin Heidegger
bio: Martin Heidegger reopened the question of the meaning of being in Being and Time, analysing human existence as Dasein; his Nazi party membership remains a central controversy.
bio_full: Martin Heidegger was born in 1889 in Messkirch, Baden, the son of a Catholic sexton, and trained for the priesthood before turning to philosophy at Freiburg. He became Husserl's assistant, taught at Marburg from 1923, where Hannah Arendt was his student and lover, and published Being and Time in 1927. He succeeded Husserl at Freiburg in 1928. In 1933 he joined the Nazi party and became rector of the university, resigning after a year but remaining a member until 1945. After the war he was banned from teaching until 1951. He spent much of his time in his hut at Todtnauberg in the Black Forest and died in 1976. The publication of his 'Black Notebooks' from 2014 revealed antisemitic passages and intensified the debate about his politics.

Being and Time asks what it means to be, starting from the being for whom being is an issue: Dasein, human existence. Dasein is always already 'being-in-the-world', engaged with equipment that is 'ready-to-hand' before it is an object of theory. It is usually absorbed in the anonymous 'they', but anxiety and the anticipation of its own death can call it to authenticity. His later thought, after a 'turn', concerned language, poetry, dwelling, and modern technology as a way of revealing that reduces everything to a 'standing reserve' of resources. He shaped existentialism, hermeneutics and deconstruction.

name: Susanne Langer
bio: Susanne Langer distinguished discursive from presentational symbols and developed a theory of art as the expressive form of human feeling.
bio_full: Susanne Katherina Knauth was born in Manhattan in 1895 to German immigrant parents and grew up speaking German at home. She studied at Radcliffe College, where she was taught by Whitehead, and married the historian William Langer. Unable to win a permanent post at Harvard, which did not appoint women to its philosophy faculty, she taught at Radcliffe and elsewhere. Philosophy in a New Key (1942) became one of the best-selling philosophy books of its time. She was professor at Connecticut College from 1954 and spent her last decades on Mind: An Essay on Human Feeling (1967–82). She died in Old Lyme, Connecticut, in 1985.

Drawing on Cassirer's philosophy of symbolic forms and Whitehead, Langer argued that human beings are distinguished by symbol-making. Discursive symbols, like language, present meanings step by step; presentational symbols, like art, music and ritual, present a complex whole at once and can articulate forms of feeling that language cannot. Feeling and Form (1953) develops a theory of each art as creating a distinct 'virtual' realm, such as virtual space in painting or virtual time in music. She influenced aesthetics, music theory and the study of ritual.

name: Leo Strauss
bio: Political philosopher Leo Strauss called for careful reading of esoteric texts and a return to classical political philosophy against modern relativism.
bio_full: Leo Strauss was born in 1899 into an Orthodox Jewish family in Kirchhain, Hesse, served in the German army in the First World War, and took a doctorate at Hamburg under Ernst Cassirer. He worked at the Academy for the Science of Judaism in Berlin, writing on Spinoza. A Rockefeller fellowship took him to Paris and England in 1932, and as a Jew he did not return to Nazi Germany. He taught at the New School for Social Research in New York from 1938 and at the University of Chicago from 1949 to 1969, and died in Annapolis in 1973.

In Persecution and the Art of Writing (1952) Strauss argued that philosophers living under persecution often wrote esoterically, conveying their real views between the lines to careful readers. Natural Right and History (1953) argued that modern social science, by denying that values can be rationally known, leads to relativism and nihilism, and called for a revival of the classical idea of natural right. He described modernity as unfolding in 'three waves', associated with Machiavelli and Hobbes, Rousseau, and Nietzsche. His students became an influential school, and claims about his influence on American politics are much disputed.

name: Gilbert Ryle
bio: In The Concept of Mind, Gilbert Ryle attacked Descartes's 'ghost in the machine' and distinguished knowing how from knowing that.
bio_full: Gilbert Ryle was born in Brighton in 1900, the son of a doctor with philosophical interests, and studied at Queen's College, Oxford. He spent his whole career at Oxford, apart from wartime service in intelligence, becoming Waynflete Professor of Metaphysical Philosophy in 1945, and edited the journal Mind from 1947 to 1971. He was a dominant figure in postwar Oxford philosophy and helped establish its graduate degree in philosophy. He died in 1976.

The Concept of Mind (1949) argues that Cartesian dualism rests on a 'category mistake', like a visitor who sees the colleges and libraries of Oxford and asks where the university is. Talk of mental states is not about an inner ghost but about dispositions to behave in certain ways. Knowing how to do something is not reducible to knowing facts. His approach is associated with ordinary language philosophy and logical behaviourism, though he resisted labels. His notion of 'thick description' was taken up by the anthropologist Clifford Geertz.

name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
bio: In Truth and Method, Hans-Georg Gadamer argued that understanding is a 'fusion of horizons' between interpreter and tradition, founding philosophical hermeneutics.
bio_full: Hans-Georg Gadamer was born in Marburg in 1900, the son of a chemistry professor, and grew up in Breslau. He studied in Marburg and was decisively influenced by Heidegger, under whom he wrote his habilitation on Plato's ethics. He taught at Leipzig, where he became rector after the war, then Frankfurt, and from 1949 Heidelberg. Truth and Method appeared in 1960, when he was sixty. He continued to lecture and debate, with Habermas and Derrida among others, until shortly before his death in Heidelberg in 2002 at the age of 102.

Gadamer argued that understanding is not a method for neutralising the interpreter's standpoint but an event in which the interpreter's historically formed horizon meets and merges with that of the text, a fusion of horizons. Prejudices, in the sense of pre-judgments, are a condition of understanding rather than simply an obstacle, and we always stand within a tradition whose 'effective history' shapes us. Understanding is dialogical, like a conversation, and the model is the experience of art. His hermeneutics influenced theology, law, literary theory and the social sciences.

name: Karl Popper
bio: Karl Popper replaced verification with falsifiability as the mark of science and defended the 'open society' against totalitarian theories of history.
bio_full: Karl Raimund Popper was born in Vienna in 1902 into a family of Jewish origin that had converted to Lutheranism. He was briefly a Marxist as a teenager, trained as a cabinetmaker and schoolteacher, and took a doctorate in psychology. Close to but critical of the Vienna Circle, he published Logik der Forschung in 1934 (translated as The Logic of Scientific Discovery in 1959). Fearing the Nazis, he took a lectureship in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1937, where he wrote The Open Society and Its Enemies. From 1946 he taught at the London School of Economics. He was knighted in 1965 and died in London in 1994.

Popper argued that no number of observations can verify a universal theory, but a single counter-instance can refute it; scientific theories are bold conjectures that must be falsifiable, and science advances by trying to refute them. Theories such as Marxism and psychoanalysis, which can accommodate any evidence, are therefore not scientific. The Open Society attacked Plato, Hegel and Marx as enemies of an open, self-critical society, and The Poverty of Historicism rejected claims to know the laws of history. He favoured piecemeal social engineering over utopian planning.

name: The Vienna Circle
bio: The Vienna Circle of philosophers and scientists held that statements are meaningful only if logically true or empirically verifiable, and sought a unified science.
bio_full: The Vienna Circle met from 1924 around the physicist and philosopher Moritz Schlick at the University of Vienna. Its members included Rudolf Carnap, Otto Neurath, Herbert Feigl, Friedrich Waismann and the mathematician Hans Hahn, with Kurt Gödel attending; a sister group in Berlin included Hans Reichenbach and Carl Hempel. In 1929 it issued a manifesto, The Scientific Conception of the World, and from 1930 published the journal Erkenntnis. Members discussed Wittgenstein's Tractatus closely, and A. J. Ayer visited and popularised their views in Language, Truth and Logic (1936). The rise of Nazism and the murder of Schlick by a former student in 1936 broke up the group; most members, many of them Jewish or socialist, emigrated to Britain and the United States.

The Circle's logical positivism, or logical empiricism, held that meaningful statements are either analytic, true by logic and meaning, or verifiable by experience; metaphysical, theological and ethical claims are therefore literally meaningless. Philosophy's task is the logical clarification of science, and all sciences should be unified in a single language. Debates over protocol sentences and the status of the verification principle itself weakened the doctrine, and Quine's attack on the analytic-synthetic distinction is often seen as its end. In America, émigré members shaped the philosophy of science for decades.

name: The Frankfurt School
bio: The Frankfurt School's critical theory, led by Max Horkheimer and Theodor Adorno, asked why Enlightenment reason and mass culture had produced new forms of domination.
bio_full: The Institute for Social Research was founded in Frankfurt in 1923 as a centre of Marxist scholarship. Under Max Horkheimer (1895–1973), its director from 1930, it brought together philosophers, sociologists, economists and psychoanalysts, including Theodor W. Adorno (1903–1969), Herbert Marcuse, Erich Fromm, Leo Lowenthal and Friedrich Pollock, with Walter Benjamin as an associate. Mostly Jewish and leftist, its members were forced into exile in 1933, moving via Geneva to Columbia University in New York and later to California. Horkheimer and Adorno returned to Frankfurt after the war and re-established the Institute in 1950. Jürgen Habermas (born 1929) led its second generation.

Horkheimer's 1937 essay 'Traditional and Critical Theory' defined a theory aimed not only at describing society but at emancipation. In Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944, revised 1947), Horkheimer and Adorno argued that Enlightenment reason, in mastering nature, had become instrumental reason that dominates human beings as well, and that the 'culture industry' produces standardised entertainment that secures conformity. Adorno's Minima Moralia and Negative Dialectics developed these themes, while Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man inspired the New Left. Habermas rebuilt the project around communicative reason and the public sphere.

name: Jean-Paul Sartre
bio: Jean-Paul Sartre, existentialism's leading public figure, held that existence precedes essence, that we are condemned to be free, and that we flee freedom in bad faith.
bio_full: Jean-Paul Sartre was born in Paris in 1905 and raised largely by his maternal grandfather, a German teacher related to Albert Schweitzer. At the École Normale Supérieure he met Simone de Beauvoir, his lifelong partner. He taught philosophy in lycées, studied Husserl in Berlin in 1933–34, and published the novel Nausea (1938). Captured as a soldier in 1940, he spent nine months as a prisoner of war. Being and Nothingness appeared in 1943, and after the Liberation his lecture 'Existentialism Is a Humanism' (1945) made him a celebrity. He founded the review Les Temps modernes, wrote plays, moved toward Marxism in the Critique of Dialectical Reason (1960), and campaigned against the Algerian and Vietnam wars. He refused the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964 and died in Paris in 1980; some fifty thousand people followed his funeral procession.

Sartre held that for human beings existence precedes essence: there is no human nature fixed in advance, and we make ourselves by our choices. Consciousness is a 'nothingness' that is always beyond what it is, so we are condemned to be free and wholly responsible. Bad faith is the attempt to escape this freedom by pretending to be a thing, like the waiter who plays at being a waiter. Relations with others are marked by the look, in which I become an object for another's freedom. His later work sought to reconcile existential freedom with Marxist history.

name: Hannah Arendt
bio: Hannah Arendt analysed totalitarianism, defended politics as speech and action among equals, and coined the phrase 'the banality of evil'.
bio_full: Hannah Arendt was born in 1906 in Linden, now part of Hanover, into a secular Jewish family and grew up in Königsberg. She studied with Heidegger at Marburg, with whom she had a love affair, with Husserl, and with Jaspers at Heidelberg, who supervised her dissertation on Augustine's concept of love. Arrested briefly by the Gestapo in 1933, she fled to Paris, where she worked for Zionist organisations, was interned in 1940 at Gurs, and escaped to the United States in 1941. Stateless until 1951, she published The Origins of Totalitarianism that year, then The Human Condition (1958). Her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann for The New Yorker, published as Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), provoked a furious controversy. She taught at Chicago and the New School and died in New York in 1975.

Arendt argued that totalitarianism, in its Nazi and Stalinist forms, was a new kind of rule, using terror and ideology to make human beings superfluous, prepared by antisemitism, imperialism and the breakdown of the nation-state. The Human Condition distinguishes labour, work and action, and holds that action, speech and deeds among plural equals in a public space, is the essence of politics, threatened in modern society. Eichmann struck her not as a monster but as thoughtless, a bureaucrat whose evil was banal. How accurate this reading of Eichmann was is still argued. Her work on judgment, revolution and the life of the mind remains widely discussed.

name: Emmanuel Levinas
bio: Emmanuel Levinas argued that ethics is first philosophy: the face of the other person commands us before any theory or knowledge.
bio_full: Emmanuel Levinas was born in 1906 into a Jewish family in Kaunas, Lithuania, and studied at Strasbourg and then at Freiburg with Husserl and Heidegger, helping to introduce phenomenology to France. He became a French citizen in 1931. Serving as an interpreter in the French army, he was captured in 1940 and spent the war in a prisoner-of-war camp for Jewish soldiers, while most of his family in Lithuania were murdered. After the war he directed a Jewish teachers' school in Paris, studied the Talmud, and published Totality and Infinity (1961) and Otherwise than Being (1974). He taught at Poitiers, Nanterre and the Sorbonne and died in Paris in 1995.

Levinas held that Western philosophy has reduced the other to the same, grasping everything within a totality of knowledge or being. In the face-to-face encounter, the face of the other person expresses a demand that precedes and exceeds any concept: 'thou shalt not kill'. My responsibility for the other is infinite and asymmetrical, and the ethical relation is prior to ontology. His work influenced Derrida, theology and ethics, and he wrote extensively on Jewish thought.

name: Simone de Beauvoir
bio: Simone de Beauvoir worked out an existentialist ethics of ambiguity and, in The Second Sex, showed how women are made the Other, opening modern feminist philosophy.
bio_full: Simone de Beauvoir was born in Paris in 1908 into a bourgeois Catholic family whose fortunes declined after the First World War. She studied philosophy at the Sorbonne and in 1929 came second, after Sartre, in the agrégation examination, becoming at twenty-one one of the youngest people ever to pass it. She and Sartre formed a lifelong partnership that rejected marriage and exclusivity. She taught in lycées until 1943, when she was dismissed after a complaint by a pupil's mother. Her novel She Came to Stay (1943), The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), The Second Sex (1949), the Goncourt-winning novel The Mandarins (1954), memoirs and Old Age (1970) followed. She campaigned for abortion rights in the 1970s and died in Paris in 1986.

The Ethics of Ambiguity argues that human beings are both free and situated, and that to will oneself free is to will others free too. The Second Sex holds that 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman': womanhood is not a natural destiny but a situation produced by history, myth and upbringing, in which man is defined as the subject and woman as the Other. She analysed biology, psychoanalysis, history, literature and women's lived experience from girlhood to old age. Long treated as Sartre's follower, she is now recognised as an original philosopher who influenced him.

name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
bio: Maurice Merleau-Ponty made the lived body the centre of phenomenology: perception is not something a mind does to data but something an embodied being lives.
bio_full: Maurice Merleau-Ponty was born in 1908 at Rochefort-sur-Mer; his father died when he was a child. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure alongside Sartre and Beauvoir, taught in lycées, and served as an infantry officer in 1939–40. The Structure of Behaviour (1942) and Phenomenology of Perception (1945) established his reputation. He co-edited Les Temps modernes with Sartre until their break over politics in the 1950s. He taught at Lyon and the Sorbonne, where he held the chair of child psychology, and from 1952 at the Collège de France, the youngest philosopher appointed there. He died suddenly in Paris in 1961, leaving The Visible and the Invisible unfinished.

Phenomenology of Perception argues against both empiricism and intellectualism that perception is the primary way we are in the world, and that the subject of perception is the lived body, with its habits, motor skills and 'body schema', drawing on case studies such as phantom limbs. The world is given to us before reflection, with meaning already in it. His late work developed an ontology of 'flesh', the shared fabric of the perceiver and the perceived. He has strongly influenced cognitive science, the philosophy of mind and feminist theory.

name: W. V. O. Quine
bio: W. V. O. Quine rejected the analytic-synthetic distinction in 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism', saw knowledge as a web of belief, and argued that epistemology should become part of natural science.
bio_full: Willard Van Orman Quine was born in Akron, Ohio, in 1908 and studied mathematics at Oberlin and then philosophy at Harvard under Whitehead. A travelling fellowship in 1932–33 took him to Vienna, Prague, where he met Carnap, and Warsaw. He joined the Harvard faculty in 1936 and stayed until his retirement in 1978, apart from naval intelligence work in the Second World War. His major works include 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951), Word and Object (1960) and 'Epistemology Naturalized' (1969). He died in Boston in 2000.

Quine argued that there is no sharp line between statements true by meaning and statements true by experience, and that our beliefs face the tribunal of experience 'not individually but only as a corporate body': any belief, even logic, could in principle be revised. Word and Object argued for the indeterminacy of translation, and his slogan 'to be is to be the value of a variable' set a standard for ontology. Philosophy is continuous with science, and epistemology should study how humans actually form theories. He was the most influential American analytic philosopher of the later twentieth century.

name: Simone Weil
bio: Simone Weil wrote on attention, affliction and the need for roots, from inside factory labour, war and exile, at the crossing of Platonism, Marxism and Christian mysticism.
bio_full: Simone Weil was born in Paris in 1909 into a secular Jewish family; her brother André became a famous mathematician. She studied with the philosopher Alain and at the École Normale Supérieure, then taught philosophy in provincial lycées while supporting workers' movements. In 1934–35 she worked in factories, including at Renault, to understand industrial labour. She joined the anarchist militia briefly in the Spanish Civil War. Mystical experiences from 1937 drew her to Christ, though she refused baptism. Fleeing with her family in 1942 to New York, she went on to London to work for the Free French, and died of tuberculosis and self-starvation at Ashford in Kent in 1943, aged thirty-four. Almost all her major work was published after her death.

Weil held that attention, a patient, receptive openness to reality and to others, is the core of both study and love, and the rarest form of generosity. Affliction (malheur), the combination of suffering, social degradation and physical pain, crushes the soul, and only attention can perceive the afflicted. Gravity, the force of self-interest and power, rules the world except where grace intervenes. The Need for Roots, written for the Free French, argued that obligations come before rights. Albert Camus published her works, and Iris Murdoch drew heavily on her idea of attention.

name: Paul Ricoeur
bio: Paul Ricoeur joined phenomenology and hermeneutics in studies of symbol, metaphor, narrative and memory, and developed the idea of narrative identity.
bio_full: Paul Ricoeur was born in Valence in 1913 into a Protestant family; his father was killed in the First World War. He studied at Rennes and the Sorbonne. Captured in 1940, he spent the war in German prisoner-of-war camps, where he translated Husserl's Ideas I. He taught at Strasbourg, the Sorbonne and the new University of Nanterre, where as dean he faced student unrest in 1968–70, and for many years at the University of Chicago. His works include Freedom and Nature (1950), Freud and Philosophy (1965), The Rule of Metaphor (1975), Time and Narrative (1983–85), Oneself as Another (1990) and Memory, History, Forgetting (2000). He died in 2005.

Ricoeur held that the self comes to know itself only through the detour of interpreting signs, symbols and texts. Interpretation pulls in two directions: a hermeneutics of suspicion, exemplified by Marx, Nietzsche and Freud, and a hermeneutics of faith that restores meaning. Time and Narrative argues that narrative gives shape to the experience of time. In Oneself as Another he distinguishes sameness (idem) from selfhood (ipse), the identity shown in keeping one's word, and argues that personal identity is narrative identity. He wrote widely on ethics, justice, memory and forgiveness.

name: G. E. M. Anscombe
bio: Elizabeth Anscombe founded the modern philosophy of action with Intention and sparked the revival of virtue ethics with 'Modern Moral Philosophy'.
bio_full: Gertrude Elizabeth Margaret Anscombe was born in Limerick in 1919, where her father was serving with the British army, and grew up in London. She converted to Catholicism as a teenager and studied at St Hugh's College, Oxford, and then at Cambridge, where she became Wittgenstein's student and close friend, later a literary executor and translator of the Philosophical Investigations. She married the philosopher Peter Geach and had seven children. She taught at Somerville College, Oxford, and in 1956 publicly opposed Oxford's honorary degree for President Truman because of the atomic bombings. From 1970 to 1986 she held Wittgenstein's former chair at Cambridge. She died in 2001.

Intention (1957) analysed intentional action as action to which a certain sense of the question 'why?' applies, and remains a foundation of the philosophy of action. 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958) argued that the concepts of moral obligation and the moral 'ought' are survivals of a divine law framework no longer believed in, and that philosophy should return to an adequate philosophical psychology and the concepts of virtue. She coined the term 'consequentialism' and defended the doctrine of double effect.

name: Philippa Foot
bio: Philippa Foot defended virtue ethics and a 'natural goodness' grounded in human life, and introduced the trolley problem.
bio_full: Philippa Ruth Bosanquet was born in 1920 in Lincolnshire; her mother was a daughter of the American president Grover Cleveland. Educated privately, she studied at Somerville College, Oxford, where she befriended Iris Murdoch, and after wartime work as an economist returned to Somerville, where she taught for decades. She married the historian M. R. D. Foot. She later taught at the University of California, Los Angeles. She was an early supporter of the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief, later Oxfam. She died in Oxford on her ninetieth birthday in 2010.

Foot argued against the prevailing non-cognitivism of R. M. Hare that moral judgments are tied to facts about human good and harm. In 'The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect' (1967) she introduced the case of a runaway tram that would later be called the trolley problem. In Natural Goodness (2001) she held that virtues are to human beings what deep roots are to an oak: features needed for a creature of that kind to flourish. With Anscombe, Murdoch and Midgley she is now seen as part of a remarkable wartime Oxford circle.

name: Iris Murdoch
bio: Novelist and philosopher Iris Murdoch argued that moral life is a matter of attention and 'unselfing' before a real Good, in The Sovereignty of Good.
bio_full: Jean Iris Murdoch was born in Dublin in 1919 and grew up in London as the only child of Anglo-Irish parents. She studied classics at Somerville College, Oxford, worked in the Treasury and for the United Nations relief agency during and after the war, and studied philosophy at Cambridge, where she encountered Wittgenstein's influence. She taught philosophy at St Anne's College, Oxford, from 1948 to 1963, then devoted herself to writing; her twenty-six novels include Under the Net and The Sea, the Sea, which won the Booker Prize in 1978. She married the critic John Bayley. She developed Alzheimer's disease and died in Oxford in 1999.

Against both existentialism and the Oxford moral philosophy of her day, which focused on choice, Murdoch argued that the moral life happens mainly in what we attend to: a mother-in-law who gradually comes to see her daughter-in-law justly has acted morally without any outward act. The fat, relentless ego distorts our vision, and attention to beauty, intellectual disciplines and other people can 'unself' us. The Good is real and magnetic, a Platonic ideal, though not a personal God. Her essays, collected in The Sovereignty of Good (1970) and Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals (1992), have become central to virtue ethics and moral psychology.

name: Mary Midgley
bio: Mary Midgley grounded ethics in an evolved human nature and campaigned against reductive scientism, likening philosophy to plumbing.
bio_full: Mary Beatrice Scrutton was born in London in 1919 and grew up in Cambridge and Greenford, where her father was a chaplain. She studied classics and philosophy at Somerville College, Oxford, where she befriended Iris Murdoch, Philippa Foot and Elizabeth Anscombe. After wartime civil service work she taught briefly, then married the philosopher Geoffrey Midgley and moved to Newcastle University, where she taught until 1980. Her first book, Beast and Man, appeared in 1978 when she was nearly sixty. She continued writing into her nineties, publishing her last book, What Is Philosophy For?, shortly before her death in 2018.

Beast and Man used ethology and evolutionary theory to argue that humans are animals with a characteristic nature, and that our moral life grows out of that nature rather than in opposition to it. She attacked 'nothing-but' reductionism, from Richard Dawkins's selfish genes to visions of science as a substitute religion, in books such as Evolution as a Religion and Science as Salvation. Philosophy, she said, is like plumbing: an unnoticed system that becomes urgent when it goes wrong. She wrote widely on animals, the environment and the Gaia hypothesis.

name: John Rawls
bio: John Rawls revived political philosophy with A Theory of Justice, deriving 'justice as fairness' from principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance.
bio_full: John Bordley Rawls was born in Baltimore in 1921; two younger brothers died of illnesses caught from him as a child. He studied at Princeton and served as an infantryman in the Pacific in the Second World War, an experience that led him to lose his Christian faith. After a doctorate at Princeton and a year at Oxford, he taught at Cornell and MIT, and from 1962 at Harvard until his retirement. A Theory of Justice appeared in 1971, after two decades of work, followed by Political Liberalism (1993) and The Law of Peoples (1999). He died in 2002.

Rawls asked what principles of justice free and equal persons would choose in an 'original position' behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their place in society, talents or conception of the good. He argued they would choose equal basic liberties for all and permit social and economic inequalities only if they arise under fair equality of opportunity and benefit the least advantaged, the difference principle. Political Liberalism addressed how citizens with deeply different religious and moral views can share a just society through an 'overlapping consensus'. His work set the agenda for political philosophy, prompting replies from Nozick, the communitarians and the capabilities approach.

name: Thomas Kuhn
bio: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, Thomas Kuhn argued that science develops through paradigms, crises and revolutions rather than steady accumulation.
bio_full: Thomas Samuel Kuhn was born in Cincinnati in 1922 and studied physics at Harvard, taking a doctorate in 1949. Teaching a general-education science course under James Conant led him to study the history of science, and he realised that Aristotle's physics made sense on its own terms. He wrote The Copernican Revolution (1957), taught at Berkeley, Princeton and from 1979 MIT, and published The Structure of Scientific Revolutions in 1962. He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1996.

Kuhn argued that mature sciences work within a paradigm, a shared set of exemplary achievements, theories and methods that defines 'normal science' as puzzle-solving. Anomalies accumulate, provoke a crisis, and are resolved by a scientific revolution in which a new paradigm replaces the old; competing paradigms are in some ways incommensurable, lacking a neutral standard of comparison. Critics charged him with making science irrational, which he denied. 'Paradigm shift' entered everyday language, and the book is among the most cited academic works of the twentieth century.

name: Michel Foucault
bio: Michel Foucault showed how power produces knowledge, institutions and kinds of people, through histories of madness, the clinic, the prison and sexuality.
bio_full: Paul-Michel Foucault was born in Poitiers in 1926, the son of a surgeon, and studied at the École Normale Supérieure, where he suffered depression. He worked in Sweden, Poland and Germany, and taught in Tunisia in the late 1960s. History of Madness (1961), The Birth of the Clinic (1963) and The Order of Things (1966), a surprise best-seller, made him famous. In 1970 he was elected to the Collège de France, to a chair in the history of systems of thought. He was active in prison reform through the Prison Information Group. Discipline and Punish (1975) and the History of Sexuality (1976–84) followed. He taught often in the United States and died of an AIDS-related illness in Paris in 1984.

Foucault argued that power is not only repressive, held by a sovereign, but productive and dispersed: modern disciplinary power shapes bodies and souls through surveillance, examination and normalisation, as in Bentham's Panopticon, and the human sciences are bound up with it (power/knowledge). He described modern 'biopower' as the management of populations' life and health. His genealogical method traced the contingent origins of what seems natural. His last work turned to ancient practices of the self. He influenced history, sociology, gender studies and political theory, while critics questioned his historical claims and the normative basis of his critique.

name: Alasdair MacIntyre
bio: In After Virtue, Alasdair MacIntyre argued that modern moral language is a heap of fragments from broken traditions, and called for a return to Aristotelian virtues sustained in communities.
bio_full: Alasdair Chalmers MacIntyre was born in Glasgow in 1929 and studied classics in London and philosophy at Manchester. In his early career he was a Marxist and wrote on Marxism, Christianity and the history of ethics. He taught at Manchester, Leeds, Oxford and Essex before moving to the United States in 1970, where he held posts at Brandeis, Boston, Vanderbilt and Duke, and finally the University of Notre Dame. He became a Catholic in the 1980s. His major works are After Virtue (1981), Whose Justice? Which Rationality? (1988) and Dependent Rational Animals (1999). He died in 2025.

After Virtue begins with an imagined catastrophe in which science survives only in fragments, and argues that modern moral discourse is similar: concepts such as rights, duty and utility survive from older frameworks without the contexts that made them intelligible, so moral argument is interminable. The Enlightenment project of justifying morality independently of tradition failed. He proposed instead an account of virtues as qualities that sustain practices, the narrative unity of a life and living traditions, drawing on Aristotle and later Aquinas. He is often grouped with communitarians, a label he rejected.

name: Bernard Williams
bio: Bernard Williams challenged systematic moral theory, introducing moral luck, the integrity objection to utilitarianism and internal reasons.
bio_full: Bernard Arthur Owen Williams was born in Westcliff-on-Sea, Essex, in 1929 and studied classics at Balliol College, Oxford. After national service as a pilot in the RAF, he taught at Oxford, University College London and Bedford College, and in 1967 became Knightbridge Professor of Philosophy at Cambridge. He was Provost of King's College, Cambridge, taught at Berkeley and returned to Oxford as White's Professor of Moral Philosophy. He chaired a government committee on obscenity and film censorship (1977–79). His books include Problems of the Self (1973), Moral Luck (1981), Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy (1985), Shame and Necessity (1993) and Truth and Truthfulness (2002). He died in Rome in 2003.

Williams argued that utilitarianism ignores the integrity of agents, whose own projects and commitments cannot simply be fed into a calculation, and that a man who saves his wife rather than a stranger and justifies it impartially has 'one thought too many'. 'Moral Luck' showed how our moral standing depends on factors beyond our control. He held that reasons for action must connect with an agent's existing motivations. Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy argued that 'morality', the system of obligation, is a peculiar institution, and that ethical theory cannot deliver what it promises. He drew on the Greeks and Nietzsche.

name: Judith Jarvis Thomson
bio: Judith Jarvis Thomson wrote 'A Defense of Abortion', with its famous violinist case, and named and shaped the trolley problem.
bio_full: Judith Jarvis was born in New York City in 1929; her mother was Czech-Catholic and her father Jewish, and she converted to Judaism as a child after her mother's death. She studied at Barnard College and Cambridge and took a doctorate at Columbia. She taught at Barnard and Boston University and from 1964 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she spent the rest of her career. She married the philosopher James Thomson. Her books include Rights, Restitution, and Risk (1986), The Realm of Rights (1990) and Normativity (2008). She died in 2020.

'A Defense of Abortion' (1971) granted for the sake of argument that the foetus is a person, and asked us to imagine waking up connected to a famous unconscious violinist who needs our kidneys for nine months: even if he has a right to life, she argued, that does not give him a right to use another's body. In 'Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem' (1976) and later papers she named and elaborated Foot's case, introducing the 'fat man' on the footbridge. The Realm of Rights developed a general theory of rights.

name: Jacques Derrida
bio: Jacques Derrida founded deconstruction, a way of reading that shows how texts depend on oppositions they cannot keep stable, and coined 'différance'.
bio_full: Jacques Derrida was born in 1930 into a Sephardic Jewish family in El Biar, near Algiers, and was expelled from school in 1942 under Vichy's antisemitic laws. He moved to France in 1949, studied at the École Normale Supérieure and wrote on Husserl. In 1967 he published three books, Of Grammatology, Writing and Difference and Speech and Phenomena, that made him internationally known. He taught at the École Normale Supérieure and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, and for many years at Yale, Johns Hopkins and the University of California, Irvine. A 1992 proposal to give him an honorary degree at Cambridge provoked a public protest by philosophers, though the degree was approved. He died in Paris in 2004.

Derrida argued that Western philosophy privileges presence, speech over writing, the literal over the metaphorical, the inside over the outside, and that its texts depend on these hierarchical oppositions while undermining them. Deconstruction is the patient reading that exposes this instability. 'Différance', a coinage combining differing and deferring, names the way meaning arises only from differences between signs and is never fully present. His later work turned to ethics, hospitality, forgiveness, justice and democracy. His influence on literary theory was enormous, while many analytic philosophers dismissed him as obscure.

name: Hanna Pitkin
bio: Political theorist Hanna Pitkin wrote The Concept of Representation, still the standard philosophical analysis of what it means to represent.
bio_full: Hanna Fenichel was born in Berlin in 1931, the daughter of the psychoanalyst Otto Fenichel. The family fled the Nazis and reached the United States in 1938, and she grew up in California. She took her doctorate at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1961 and spent her career there as a professor of political science and a famously demanding teacher of political theory. Her books include The Concept of Representation (1967), Wittgenstein and Justice (1972), Fortune Is a Woman (1984), on Machiavelli, and The Attack of the Blob (1998), on Arendt. She died in 2023.

The Concept of Representation distinguished formal views of representation, as authorisation or accountability, from 'standing for', whether descriptively or symbolically, and from 'acting for' others, arguing that representation means making present in some sense what is nevertheless not literally present. Wittgenstein and Justice applied ordinary language philosophy to political concepts. Her book on Machiavelli used psychoanalysis to explore his images of manhood and fortune.

name: Derek Parfit
bio: Derek Parfit argued that personal identity is not what matters in survival and founded modern population ethics, in Reasons and Persons and On What Matters.
bio_full: Derek Antony Parfit was born in 1942 in Chengdu, China, to British medical missionaries, and grew up in Oxford. He studied modern history at Balliol College, Oxford, then held fellowships in the United States before turning to philosophy. He spent his whole career as a research fellow at All Souls College, Oxford, while also teaching regularly at Harvard, New York University and Rutgers. He was an accomplished architectural photographer, especially of Venice and St Petersburg. Reasons and Persons appeared in 1984 and the three volumes of On What Matters in 2011–17. He died in London in 2017.

Using thought experiments about teleportation, brain division and gradual replacement, Parfit argued that personal identity is not a deep further fact; what matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, which can hold in degrees. Accepting this, he found, made him less concerned about his own death. He formulated the non-identity problem, that policies affecting future people also determine who will exist, and the 'repugnant conclusion' of population ethics. On What Matters argued that the best versions of Kantian, consequentialist and contractualist ethics converge, 'climbing the same mountain on different sides', and defended objective moral truths.

name: Peter Singer
bio: Peter Singer argued for a demanding duty to aid the global poor and against 'speciesism' in Animal Liberation, and is a leading public utilitarian.
bio_full: Peter Albert David Singer was born in Melbourne in 1946 to Jewish parents who had fled Vienna; three of his grandparents were killed in the Holocaust. He studied at the University of Melbourne and at Oxford, where he joined a group of vegetarian students and wrote Animal Liberation (1975). He taught at Oxford, New York University, La Trobe and Monash universities, and from 1999 at Princeton, where his appointment was met with protests over his views on disability and infanticide. Other books include Practical Ethics (1979), The Life You Can Save (2009) and The Most Good You Can Do (2015).

'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972) argued that if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it, like saving a child drowning in a shallow pond at the cost of muddy clothes; distance makes no moral difference. Animal Liberation argued that the capacity to suffer, not species membership, is what counts morally, and that factory farming and much animal experimentation are unjustifiable. For most of his career a preference utilitarian, he later defended hedonistic utilitarianism. He was a major influence on the animal rights and effective altruism movements, and his views on euthanasia and disability remain controversial.

name: Martha Nussbaum
bio: Martha Nussbaum developed the capabilities approach to justice, treats emotions as judgments of value, and reads Greek tragedy and philosophy as resources for ethics.
bio_full: Martha Craven was born in New York City in 1947 and grew up in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania. After a period acting in repertory theatre, she studied classics at New York University and took a doctorate at Harvard. She converted to Judaism on her marriage. She taught at Harvard and Brown, worked with the economist Amartya Sen at the World Institute for Development Economics Research, and since 1995 has taught law and ethics at the University of Chicago. Her books include The Fragility of Goodness (1986), Upheavals of Thought (2001), Frontiers of Justice (2006), Creating Capabilities (2011) and Anger and Forgiveness (2016).

The Fragility of Goodness argued, through Greek tragedy, Plato and Aristotle, that a good human life is vulnerable to luck. With Sen she developed the capabilities approach, which asks what people are actually able to do and to be, and proposed a list of central human capabilities, such as life, health, bodily integrity, practical reason and affiliation, that a just society must secure to a threshold for everyone; she has extended it to people with disabilities and to animals. Upheavals of Thought treats emotions as intelligent judgments about what matters to us. She is one of the most prominent public philosophers in the United States.
